(p-198) Sūrat al-A'rāf

Makkī in its entirety according to al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrima, and Jābir. Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah said: it is Makkī except for five verses, namely His saying: ﴿And ask them about the town﴾ [al-A'rāf: 163] to the end of the five.

First: its meaning is "I am Allah, the Fashioner (uṣawwir)," or "I am Allah, the Best-Judge (ufaḍḍil)." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

Second: that it is letters of the alphabet (ḥurūf hijāʾ) from "al-muṣawwir" (the Fashioner), said by al-Suddī.

Third: that it is a name of the surah, one of the names of the Qur'an, said by Qatādah.

Fourth: that it is the name of the surah and its key (miftāḥ), said by al-Ḥasan.

Fifth: that it is an abbreviation of a statement which the Prophet ﷺ understood, and this is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Sixth: they are disjointed letters of the alphabet, by which He draws attention to the inimitability (iʿjāz) of the Qur'an.

Seventh: they are from the counting of the abjad reckoning (ḥisāb al-jummal), the calculation of which Allah has reserved the knowledge of for Himself.

(p-199) Eighth: they are letters containing many meanings, by which Allah, the Exalted, informed His creation of His intended meaning from all of that.

Ninth: they are the letters of Allah's Greatest Name (al-ism al-aʿẓam).

In my view, a tenth opinion is possible: that what is meant by it is "the destination (al-maṣīr) to a Book that has been sent down to you from your Lord," so the rest of the word has been omitted by apocope (tarkhīm), and it is expressed by the letters of the alphabet, because these letters carry the listener in every direction. The Arabs have a way of confining themselves to letters, as the poet said:

"I said to her: 'Stop (qifī),' and she said: 'Qāf.'"

... ... ...

That is, "I stopped (waqaftu)."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿A Book that has been sent down to you﴾ means the Qur'an.

﴿So let there be no constriction (ḥaraj) in your breast concerning it﴾. Regarding ḥaraj here there are three opinions: First: that it means narrowness (ḍīq), said by al-Ḥasan, and this is its root meaning.

al-Shammākh ibn Ḍirār said:

"Even if he returned the kindness to me, I would return it, [for a need], not as the lofty nor as the one who is distressed (al-mutaḥarrij)."

And its meaning would be: "let your breast not be constricted for fear that you will not fulfil its right."

Second: that ḥaraj here means doubt, said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and al-Suddī.

The reciter (rājiz) said:

"I swore, were it not for a ḥaraj that besets me, I would not have come to raid you, nor would you raid me."

Its meaning: "do not doubt regarding what is binding upon you in it, for it was sent down to you so that you may warn by it."

Third: "let your breast not be constricted by their denying you," said by al-Farrāʾ.

Then He said: ﴿That you may warn thereby, and as a reminder for the believers﴾. He made it a warning for the disbelievers and a reminder for the believers, so that its benefit returns to both groups.(p-200)

The Exalted said: ﴿How many a town We destroyed!﴾ and so on. This is an account from God, exalted is He, about the state of those whom He destroyed for their disbelief, as a warning to those addressed by it against the like of it.

His words ﴿How many [kam]﴾ are a word used for multiplicity, while *rubba* (a particle of paucity) is used for fewness. That is the difference between *kam* and *rubba*.

Al-Farazdaq said:

> How many an aunt you have, O Jarir, and how many a maternal aunt, a wet-nurse who has milked my she-camels!

This indicates the multiplicity of aunts and maternal aunts.

As for His words ﴿We destroyed them, and Our might came upon them at night [bayatan]﴾, the destruction following the coming of the might [ba's] has four aspects:

First: its meaning is "We destroyed them in judgment, and Our might came upon them in action."

Second: "We destroyed them by sending the angels to them with the punishment, and Our might came upon them in the occurrence of the punishment against them."

Third: "We destroyed them by abandoning them, withdrawing Our support from them in obedience, and Our might came upon them as a punishment for disobedience."

Fourth: that the might [ba's] and the destruction occurred together in a single state, because the destruction took place through the occurrence of the might, so they were not separate. The insertion of the *fa* (then) between them does not necessarily require their separation; rather it may carry the meaning of *wa* (and), as one says, "You gave and you did good," where the doing of good was by the giving and not after it. This was said by al-Farra'.

His words ﴿at night [bayatan]﴾ mean during the sleep of the night.

﴿Or while they were taking their midday rest [qa'ilun]﴾ mean during the sleep of the day, at the time of the midday rest.

If it is said: why did He bring the punishment upon them at the time of sleep rather than when they were awake? It is answered: for two reasons. One: because punishment at the time of rest is more severe and harsher.

(p-201) The second: so that they could not guard against it and flee from it, since the sleeper is helpless while the one awake is on his guard. *Al-ba's* means the severity of punishment, and *al-bu's* means the severity of poverty.

The Exalted said: ﴿Then We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾. In this there are two views:

First: We will surely question those to whom the messengers were sent about accepting the message and fulfilling its conditions, and We will surely question the messengers about delivering the message and being trustworthy in it.

Second: We will surely question those to whom the messengers were sent about preserving the messengers' rights, and We will surely question the messengers about their compassion toward the nations.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 8–9:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: the weighing here means the judgment with truth, that is, with justice. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it is the weighing of good deeds and bad deeds by signs that people will see on the Day of Resurrection.

The third: it is the weighing of good deeds and bad deeds by a balance that has two pans. This was said by al-Hasan and a group.

Those who held this view differed about what is weighed, on three opinions. The first: what is weighed is the good deeds and bad deeds, by placing one of them in a pan and the other in a pan. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

The second: what is weighed is the pages of the deeds, since good deeds and bad deeds are themselves actions, and weighing is only possible for bodies. This was said by Abdullah ibn Umar.

The third: what is weighed is the human being. Ubayd ibn Umayr said: a man of enormous body will be brought, yet he will not weigh the wing of a mosquito.

(p-202) ﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: its meaning is whoever is decreed to have obedience (to his credit).

The second: its meaning is whoever's pan of good deeds is heavier than the pan of his bad deeds.

The third: its meaning is whoever's good deeds exceed his bad deeds.

﴿Those are the successful﴾ means by what they have of reward, and the opposite when (the scales) are light.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And We have certainly established you upon the earth﴾, has two interpretations. The first: We made its management easy for you, until you reached your aims from it.

The second: We gave you ownership of it, until you became more entitled to it.

﴿And We made for you therein means of livelihood﴾, has two interpretations. The first: that by which you live, of plants and animals.

The second: that by which you attain your livelihoods therein, of farming or work.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And We certainly created you, then We formed you﴾. Concerning this, the people of ta'wil (interpretation) have four opinions. The first: "And We certainly created you" means in the loins of men, "then We formed you" means in the wombs of women. This is the view of Ikrimah.

The second: "And We certainly created you" means Adam, "then We formed you" means in his back. This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: "We created you" as drops of semen in the loins of men and the breastbones of women, "then We formed you" at the joining of the two drops in the wombs. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Kalbi.

(p-203) The fourth: "We created you" in the bellies of your mothers, "then We formed you" within them after creation by splitting the hearing and the sight. This is the view of Ma'mar.

﴿Then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾. If it is said: prostration is an act of worship that is not permissible except to Allah, the Exalted, so how was it commanded for Adam, peace be upon him? It is said: concerning this, the scholars have two opinions. The first: He commanded them to prostrate to him as an honour, and it is an act of worship to Allah, the Exalted. The second: He made him the qiblah (direction) of their prostration to Allah, the Exalted.

If it is said: the command to prostrate to Adam came before the forming of his descendants, so how did He say: ﴿then We formed you, then We said to the angels, "Prostrate"﴾? In response to this there are three answers. The first: He formed them in the loins of Adam, then He said to the angels: Prostrate.

The second: its meaning is "then We formed you, then We informed you that We said to the angels: Prostrate."

The third: that there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech, and its estimation is: "Then We said to the angels, Prostrate to Adam, then We formed you."

There is a fourth answer, which some grammarians denied, namely that "thumma" (then) here carries the meaning of "wa" (and). This is the view of al-Akhfash.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 7, verses 12–15:**

(p-٢០٤) His, may He be exalted and majestic, saying: ﴿He said, "Then descend from it"﴾. There are three opinions concerning it. The first: he was sent down from the heaven, because he had been in it. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: from the Garden (al-Jannah).

The third: he was brought down from the lofty station that he had earned through obedience to God to the lowly station that he deserved through disobedience to Him. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿So it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾. No created being may be arrogant therein or anywhere else. Rather, the meaning is: it is not for one who is arrogant to be therein, and the arrogant one belongs outside of it.

Concerning the arrogance there are two aspects. The first: arrogance toward God, by refusing to submit to Him. The second: arrogance toward Adam, by refusing to prostrate to him.

﴿Then get out﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: from the place in which he was, whether the heaven or the Garden. The second: from the company of the angels among whom he was, or who were with him.

﴿Indeed, you are of the debased﴾. Concerning this there are two aspects. The first: debased in this world by disobedience, since the disobedient is humiliated in the sight of the one he disobeys. The second: debased in the Hereafter by punishment, since the one who is punished is humiliated by the punishment.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 16–17:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿He said, "Because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path.﴾ The scholars of Arabic (ahl al-'arabiyyah, the grammarians) differed over the meaning of His saying ﴿Because You have led me astray (fa-bima aghwaytani)﴾ according to two views:

(p-206) The first: it is in the sense of an oath, and its estimated meaning is: "By Your leading me astray, I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path."

The second: it is in the sense of a conditional consequence (mujazah), its estimated meaning being: "Because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path."

The scholars differed over His saying ﴿You have led me astray (aghwaytani)﴾ in four statements:

The first: its meaning is "You have misguided me," said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd.

The second: its meaning is "You have deprived me of Your garden," and from it is the saying of the poet:

؎ Whoever meets good, people praise his affair, and whoever goes astray (yaghu) will not lack a blamer for his error.

That is, whoever is disappointed (yakhib).

The third: its meaning is "You have punished me," like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they will meet ghayy (destruction)﴾ [Maryam: 59], meaning punishment, said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: its meaning is "You have destroyed me by Your curse upon me." It is said "ghawa al-fasil" when the young camel is brought near to death from loss of milk. The poet said:

؎ Bent in its ribs, its young one is not one who takes from her milk, nor is it a dead one that has perished.

As for His saying ﴿sit in ambush for them on Your straight path﴾, that is, upon Your straight path, and in it there are two interpretations: The first: the road to Makkah, so that he may bar them from its pilgrimage and 'umrah, said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: the path of truth, so that he may bar them from it through misguidance, said by Mujahid.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾ and the rest of the verse.

In it there are four interpretations: The first: ﴿from before them﴾ means: I will cast doubt upon them regarding their Hereafter; ﴿and from behind them﴾ (p-207): I will make their worldly life appealing to them; ﴿and from their right﴾: that is, from the side of their good deeds; ﴿and from their left﴾: from the side of their bad deeds, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: ﴿from before them﴾: from the side of their worldly life; ﴿and from behind them﴾: from the side of their Hereafter; ﴿and from their right﴾: the truth, about which I will cast doubt upon them; ﴿and from their left﴾: falsehood, toward which I will make them eager, said by al-Suddi and Ibrahim.

The third: ﴿from before them﴾ and ﴿from their right﴾: from where they can see; ﴿from behind them﴾ and ﴿from their left﴾: from where they cannot see, said by Mujahid.

The fourth: he meant from all the directions from which it is possible to scheme against them. He did not mention "from above them" because God's mercy repels him, nor "from beneath their feet" because of what it contains of causing aversion, said by some of the later scholars.

It may also bear a fifth interpretation: ﴿from before them﴾: concerning what remains of their lifespans, so that they do not advance to obedience; ﴿and from behind them﴾: concerning what has passed of their lifespans, so that they do not repent of disobedience; ﴿and from their right﴾: from the side of their wealth, so that they do not spend it in what is praiseworthy; ﴿and from their left﴾: from the side of their poverty, so that they do not refrain in it from what is forbidden.

It may also bear a sixth: ﴿from before them﴾: the spreading of their hopes; ﴿and from behind them﴾: the enthroning of their ignorance; ﴿and from their right﴾: in what is made easy for them; ﴿and from their left﴾: in what is made difficult for them. Then He said: ﴿and You will not find most of them grateful﴾, which has two possible meanings: The first: grateful for Your blessings. The second: steadfast in Your obedience.

If it is asked: how did Iblis know that? There are two answers to it: The first: he presumed it and his presumption proved true, as Exalted is He said: ﴿And Iblis did indeed confirm his assumption about them﴾ [Saba': 20]. The cause of his presumption was that when he misled Adam and caused him to slip, he said: "The offspring of this one are weaker than him," said by al-Hasan.

The second: it is possible that he knew that from the angels, by a report from God.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Go forth from it﴾ admits of two interpretations. The first: from the place where you were, whether a garden or a heaven.

The second: from obedience, in the manner of a threat.

﴿Disgraced and expelled﴾. Regarding His saying ﴿disgraced﴾ (mad'ūman), there are five interpretations. The first: it means blameworthy (madhmūman), said by Ibn Zayd. al-A'mash recited it as ma'ūman (madhūman). The second: despicable (la'īman), said by al-Kalbi. The third: loathed (maqītan), said by Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: banished (manfiyyan), said by Mujahid. The fifth: that it is an intensified form of censure, which is worse in state than the blameworthy (madhmūm), said by al-Akhfash. 'Amir ibn Judhama said:

Judhama did not take the truth; rather their hearts swerved before the fighting, reviled (dha'aman).

As for ﴿expelled﴾ (madhūran, al-madhhūr), there are two views. The first: pushed away (al-madfū'). The second: driven out (al-mazṭūd), said by Mujahid and al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 19–21:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾. He means Hawwa' (Eve). Concerning the Garden in which he was commanded to dwell, there are two opinions. (p-209) One: it is the Garden of Eternity (jannat al-khuld) which the God-fearing have been promised, and leaving it was permissible because it was not made a reward in which one would abide forever and never leave.

The second: it is one of the gardens of this world, in which there is no obligation (taklif), though he was under obligation.

﴿So eat from wherever you wish﴾ may bear two meanings. One: from wherever you wish of the Garden in its entirety.

The second: whatever fruits you wish of all the fruits, because the thing excluded by the prohibition was a fruit, so the thing permitted was a fruit.

﴿But do not approach this tree﴾. We have already mentioned the people's disagreement concerning it, in six opinions. The first: it is wheat, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the vine, said by al-Suddi.

The third: the fig, said by Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth: the tree of camphor, said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The fifth: the tree of knowledge, said by al-Kalbi.

The sixth: that it is the tree of eternity from which the angels eat, said by Ibn Ju'dan. Muhammad ibn Ishaq related from the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitabayn) that it is the colocynth tree, but I do not know a basis for this.

If it is said: What is the reason for forbidding them from it, given their perfect knowledge? It is said: the benefit lies in the continuation of knowledge, and in being tested by that which requires reward or punishment.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Then Satan whispered to them to reveal to them﴾. As for waswasa (whispering), it is the concealing of the voice in supplication. It is said: waswasa lahu when he gave him a false impression of advice, and waswasa ilayhi when he cast the meaning to him. On this is the verse of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj:

؎ He whispered, supplicating sincerely the Lord of the daybreak, secretly, and he had murmured the murmuring of the ʻaqaq.

(p-210) If it is asked: How did he whisper to them while they were in the Garden and he was outside it? There are three answers concerning this, which are opinions over which the exegetes differed. One: he whispered to them while they were in the Garden in the heaven, while he was on the earth, and his whispering reached them by the power God created in him, up to the heaven and then the Garden; this was said by al-Hasan.

The second: that he was in the heaven, and they would come out to him and meet him there.

The third: that he addressed them from the gate of the Garden while they were within it.

﴿And he said: Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become of the immortals﴾. This is what he cast into them as whispering, seducing them by encouraging them toward the excellence of rank and the bliss of eternity.

If it is asked: Did they imagine that, given their perfect knowledge? It is said: their knowledge of God, Exalted is He, was perfect, but not of His rulings.

Concerning Iblis's saying that, there are two opinions. One: he gave them the false impression that it was permissible in God's ruling for Him to transform their forms into the forms of angels and to make them abide forever in the Garden.

The second: he gave them the false impression that they would become like the angels in elevation of rank, while knowing that the transformation of forms is not permissible.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And he swore to them: Indeed I am to you of the sincere advisers﴾. That is, he swore to them of the truth of his report and the sincerity of his counsel, so they accepted his word and imagined his truthfulness, because they did not know that anyone would dare to swear falsely by God.

It may bear another meaning: that the meaning of His saying ﴿And he swore to them﴾ is that he said to them: If what I have said is good, then it is for you rather than me, and if it is evil, then it is upon me rather than you; and whoever does this with you is among the sincere advisers to you. So this was his swearing to them: that he allotted the good to them and the evil to himself, in a manner of deception, so that suspicion would be removed from him and acceptance would come to him quickly. (p-211)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 19–21:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾. He means Hawwa' (Eve). Concerning the Garden in which he was commanded to dwell, there are two opinions. (p-209) One: it is the Garden of Eternity (jannat al-khuld) which the God-fearing have been promised, and leaving it was permissible because it was not made a reward in which one would abide forever and never leave.

The second: it is one of the gardens of this world, in which there is no obligation (taklif), though he was under obligation.

﴿So eat from wherever you wish﴾ may bear two meanings. One: from wherever you wish of the Garden in its entirety.

The second: whatever fruits you wish of all the fruits, because the thing excluded by the prohibition was a fruit, so the thing permitted was a fruit.

﴿But do not approach this tree﴾. We have already mentioned the people's disagreement concerning it, in six opinions. The first: it is wheat, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the vine, said by al-Suddi.

The third: the fig, said by Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth: the tree of camphor, said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

The fifth: the tree of knowledge, said by al-Kalbi.

The sixth: that it is the tree of eternity from which the angels eat, said by Ibn Ju'dan. Muhammad ibn Ishaq related from the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitabayn) that it is the colocynth tree, but I do not know a basis for this.

If it is said: What is the reason for forbidding them from it, given their perfect knowledge? It is said: the benefit lies in the continuation of knowledge, and in being tested by that which requires reward or punishment.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Then Satan whispered to them to reveal to them﴾. As for waswasa (whispering), it is the concealing of the voice in supplication. It is said: waswasa lahu when he gave him a false impression of advice, and waswasa ilayhi when he cast the meaning to him. On this is the verse of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj:

؎ He whispered, supplicating sincerely the Lord of the daybreak, secretly, and he had murmured the murmuring of the ʻaqaq.

(p-210) If it is asked: How did he whisper to them while they were in the Garden and he was outside it? There are three answers concerning this, which are opinions over which the exegetes differed. One: he whispered to them while they were in the Garden in the heaven, while he was on the earth, and his whispering reached them by the power God created in him, up to the heaven and then the Garden; this was said by al-Hasan.

The second: that he was in the heaven, and they would come out to him and meet him there.

The third: that he addressed them from the gate of the Garden while they were within it.

﴿And he said: Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become of the immortals﴾. This is what he cast into them as whispering, seducing them by encouraging them toward the excellence of rank and the bliss of eternity.

If it is asked: Did they imagine that, given their perfect knowledge? It is said: their knowledge of God, Exalted is He, was perfect, but not of His rulings.

Concerning Iblis's saying that, there are two opinions. One: he gave them the false impression that it was permissible in God's ruling for Him to transform their forms into the forms of angels and to make them abide forever in the Garden.

The second: he gave them the false impression that they would become like the angels in elevation of rank, while knowing that the transformation of forms is not permissible.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And he swore to them: Indeed I am to you of the sincere advisers﴾. That is, he swore to them of the truth of his report and the sincerity of his counsel, so they accepted his word and imagined his truthfulness, because they did not know that anyone would dare to swear falsely by God.

It may bear another meaning: that the meaning of His saying ﴿And he swore to them﴾ is that he said to them: If what I have said is good, then it is for you rather than me, and if it is evil, then it is upon me rather than you; and whoever does this with you is among the sincere advisers to you. So this was his swearing to them: that he allotted the good to them and the evil to himself, in a manner of deception, so that suspicion would be removed from him and acceptance would come to him quickly. (p-211)

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So he lured them with deception﴾. Its meaning is: he brought them down, by deception, from the rank of obedience to the state of disobedience.

If it is asked: did they know, when they ate, that it was an act of disobedience? It is answered: No. For their proceeding to it while knowing that it was disobedience would make it a major sin (kabira), and the prophets are protected (ma'sumun) from major sins. They proceeded to it only because of a doubt (shubha) that entered upon them through the deception.

﴿When they tasted of the tree, their private parts became apparent to them﴾. If it is asked: why did their private parts become apparent to them, when they had not been apparent to them before? There are three answers to this:

The first: they had been covered by obedience, and the covering was removed from them by disobedience.

The second: they had been covered by the light of honour, and the humiliation (mahana) was removed from them by that.

The third: by their disobedience they left being among the inhabitants of the Garden, so what they had been in of protection (siyana) was removed from them.

﴿And they began to fasten over themselves some leaves of the Garden﴾. In ﴿and they began﴾ (wa-tafiqa) there are two aspects. The first: they stood up and began to fasten (yakhsifan), as said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: they began to fasten, meaning they cut (yaqta'an).

﴿Of the leaves of the Garden﴾. Concerning this there are two statements. The first: the leaves of the banana plant (al-mawz).

The second: the leaves of the fig tree (al-tin), as said by Ibn 'Abbas.(p-212)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 24–25:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿He said: Go down, some of you being enemies to others﴾. If it is said: the one commanded to descend is Adam and Hawwa', since Iblis had already been made to descend earlier, when he refused to prostrate to Adam, so how did He refer to them with a plural form? On this there are three answers. The first: it is a report about their descent together, even though it comes in the form of a command; this is the view of al-Suddi. The second: they are Adam, Hawwa' and the serpent, and so they were a group; this is the view of Abu Salih. The third: they are Adam, Hawwa' and the whispering (al-wiswas); this is the view of al-Hasan.

Adam descended in the land of India upon a mountain called Wasm, Hawwa' descended at Jeddah, and the serpent descended at Isfahan.

Regarding the place of Iblis's descent there are two opinions. One is al-Ubulla; the other is al-Madar.

It is also said that He made them dwell in the Garden for three hours of Friday, and expelled them after nine hours of that day had passed.

﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling-place and provision for a time﴾. As for mustaqarr (dwelling-place), there are two aspects: the first is that it is the act of settling; the second is that it is the place of settling; this is the view of Abu Salih. As for mata' (provision), it is what is benefited from among the goods of this world by which one enjoys oneself.

His saying: ﴿for a time﴾ means until the end of the world. Hin (a time) is a period of unknown extent that applies to both long and short duration, although it is generally used for a large amount.

(p-213) The poet said:

And what is your jesting after dreams and religion, when the white hair of an age that is not an age has overtaken you?

That is: a time that is not a time.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 26:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts﴾. This verse was revealed concerning a people of the Arabs who used to circumambulate the House naked, and they considered that this was more eloquent in obedience and greater in nearness to God.

Regarding the entry of doubt upon them in this matter, there are two aspects. The first: clothes had been defiled by sins, so they removed themselves from them.

The second: as an omen of being stripped of sins. So God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿We have sent down to you clothing﴾, meaning what you wear of garments.

If it is said: that is not sent down from the sky.

Then there are two answers to this. The first: since it grows from the rain that descended from the sky, it becomes as though sent down from the sky. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: that this is among the blessings of God, and blessing is attributed to descending from the sky, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And We sent down iron﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. Then He said: ﴿to cover your private parts﴾, meaning it conceals your nakedness. The nakedness (ʿawrah) was called sawʾah because its uncovering distresses its owner (yasūʾu).

Then He said: ﴿and as adornment (rīsh)﴾. This is the reading of the people of the major cities. Al-Hasan used to recite: (wa-riyāsh). Concerning it there are four interpretations: (p-214) The first: that it is the livelihood, said by Maʿbad al-Juhani.

The second: that it is clothing, living and bounty, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: that it is beauty and adornment, said by Ibn Zayd, and from it is the verse of Ruʾbah:

"To You I complain of the hardship of livelihood and the toil of years that plucked my feathers (rīshī)"

He means: they removed my beauty and my adornment.

The fourth: that it is wealth, said by Ibn al-Zubayr and Mujahid. The poet says:

"My feathers (rīshī) are from you, and my passion is with you, even if your visits are but occasional (limām)."

Concerning rīsh and riyāsh there are two views. The first: their meaning is one, though their wording differs.

The second view: their meanings differ; rīsh is what is inward, and riyāsh is what is outward.

Then He said: ﴿and the garment of piety, that is best﴾. Concerning the garment of piety there are seven interpretations. The first: it is faith, said by Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The second: modesty, said by Maʿbad al-Juhani.

The third: righteous deed, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: good bearing, said by ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan.

The fifth: fear of God, said by ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr.

The sixth: covering the nakedness for prayer, which is piety, said by Ibn Zayd.

The seventh: wearing what protects against heat and cold, said by Ibn Bahr.

(p-215) Concerning His saying ﴿that is best﴾ there are two views. The first: it refers to the garment of piety, and the meaning of the statement is that the garment of piety is better than adornment and clothing, said by Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The second: it refers to everything mentioned before: ﴿We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts and adornment, and the garment of piety﴾. Then He said: "that" (dhalika), which I have mentioned, is "best" (khayr) in its entirety.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 27:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden﴾. This is an address directed to those among the Arabs who used to circumambulate the House naked, so it was said to them: let not Satan tempt you by his deception as he tempted your parents before you until he removed them from the Garden, so that making them aware of this would be more forceful in deterrence than the mere prohibition.

﴿He stripped them of their clothing﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: their clothing was nails that covered the body; these were stripped from them and left as adornment and a means of sight. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second: their clothing was light. This is the view of Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The third: he stripped them of their clothing of God-fearing piety and obedience to Him. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿to show them their private parts﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. One: their bodies, from the nakedness (awrah) when they came out of their clothing, and this is what the saying of Ibn Abbas implies.

The second: the shame of their disobedience, until they departed from the piety and obedience of God. This is the meaning of the saying of Mujahid.

﴿Indeed, he and his tribe see you from where you do not see them﴾. Concerning this there are two possibilities. One: his people (qawm), and this is the view of the majority.

(p-216) The second: his generation (jil), as reported by al-Suddi.

﴿from where you do not see them﴾ admits of two meanings. One: from where you cannot see their bodies. The second: from where you do not know their scheming and their temptation.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 28–30:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when they commit an indecency, they say, "We found our fathers doing it, and Allah has commanded us to it."﴾ In this verse there are three opinions. The first: it was revealed concerning the Arabs who used to circumambulate the Ka'bah naked, and the indecency they committed was the uncovering of the private parts. This is the view of most of the exegetes (mufassirun).

The second: it concerns the worshippers of idols, and the indecency they committed was shirk (associating partners with Allah). This was said by al-Hasan (al-Basri).

The third: it is the taking of the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham (practices of pre-Islamic Arabia concerning certain animals). This was said by al-Kalbi.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Say, "My Lord has commanded justice."﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations. One: it means truthfulness. The second: it means justice.

﴿And set your faces right at every place of prayer﴾ Concerning this there are four interpretations. The first: its meaning is, "Turn toward the Ka'bah in prayer wherever you are," said by Mujahid. The second: its meaning is, "Make your prostration sincerely for Allah, the Exalted, apart from anything else, such as the idols and images," said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. The third: its meaning is, "Head for the masjid at the time of every prayer, as a command to perform it in congregation; it is recommended according to the majority, and obligatory according to a minority." The fourth: wherever you find the time of prayer, pray there, for that place is a masjid, and do not delay it until you reach the masjid.

﴿And call upon Him, making your religion sincerely His﴾ This may bear two meanings. One: that is, acknowledge His oneness and sincerely devote obedience to Him. The second: supplicate to Him earnestly in du'a after your sincerity to Him in religion.

﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ Concerning this there are four opinions. The first: "As He originated you wretched and happy, so you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection," said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "As He originated you, some of you believed and some of you disbelieved, so you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection."

Abu Sufyan narrated from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Every soul will be resurrected upon what it was upon."

The third: "As He created you when you were nothing, so you will return after annihilation alive," said by al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: "As He originated you, you own nothing, so you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked and uncircumcised. The first to be clothed will be Ibrahim (peace be upon him)." Then he recited: ﴿As We originated the first creation, We will repeat it; a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We will be doing it.﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:104]

The third: its meaning is, "Head for the masjid at the time of every prayer, as a command to perform it in congregation; it is recommended according to the majority, and obligatory according to a minority." The fourth: wherever you find the time of prayer, pray there, for that place is a masjid, and do not delay it until you reach the masjid.

﴿And call upon Him, making your religion sincerely His﴾ This may bear two meanings. One: that is, acknowledge His oneness and sincerely devote obedience to Him. The second: supplicate to Him earnestly in du'a after your sincerity to Him in religion.

﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ Concerning this there are four opinions. The first: "As He originated you wretched and happy, so you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection," said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "As He originated you, some of you believed and some of you disbelieved, so you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection."

Abu Sufyan narrated from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Every soul will be resurrected upon what it was upon."

The third: "As He created you when you were nothing, so you will return after annihilation alive," said by al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: "As He originated you, you own nothing, so you will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked and uncircumcised. The first to be clothed will be Ibrahim (peace be upon him)." Then he recited: ﴿As We originated the first creation, We will repeat it; a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We will be doing it.﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:104]

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 31:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿O Children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prayer﴾. On this there are four opinions. The first: that it refers to covering the nakedness (al-'awrah) during circumambulation (tawaf), as mentioned earlier. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ata', Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Ibrahim. (p-218)

The second: that it refers to covering the nakedness during prayer. This was said by Mujahid and al-Zajjaj.

The third: that it refers to adorning oneself with the finest clothing on Friday gatherings (al-juma') and festivals.

The fourth: that it means the comb, for combing the beard.

﴿And eat and drink﴾, meaning what Allah has made lawful for you.

It may be that this is a command to be generous during festivals.

﴿And do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like the excessive﴾. On this there are three interpretations. The first: do not be excessive in what is forbidden; this was said by al-Suddi. The second: its meaning is, do not eat what is unlawful, for that is excess; this was said by Ibn Zayd. The third: do not be excessive in eating what exceeds satiety, for that is harmful; and there has come in a hadith: "The root of every disease is overeating (al-burdah)," meaning indigestion (al-tukhmah).

It may bear a fourth interpretation: do not be excessive in spending.

As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, He does not like the excessive﴾, it may bear two meanings. One: He does not like their actions of excess. The second: He does not like them, in their own selves, because of their excess.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 32:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants?﴾ He means covering the private parts (satr al-'awrah), in refutation of the Arabs' abandoning of it during the circumambulation (tawaf).

It may secondly be understood that He intends their adornment in clothing.

Then He said: ﴿and the good things of provision﴾. Concerning this there are two views. One: they used to forbid, while in the state of ihram (pilgrim's consecration), the eating of ghee and milk; this was said by Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi.

The second: it refers to the bahirah and the sa'ibah, which they forbade upon themselves; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Regarding "the good things of provision" there are two views. One: that it means what is pleasant (al-mustalidh). 

The second: that it means what is lawful (al-halal).

﴿Say: They are, for those who believed, in the life of this world, exclusively so on the Day of Resurrection﴾. He means that the good things of provision belong to those who believed in the life of this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they belong to them alone, because on the Day of Resurrection they will have them exclusively, whereas in this world the disbelievers may share them with them.

Regarding His saying ﴿exclusively so on the Day of Resurrection﴾ there are two aspects. One: exclusively theirs, to the exclusion of the disbelievers. The second: exclusive of any harm or sin.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 33:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden the indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: the indecencies (al-fawahish) are specifically fornication (al-zina), what is apparent of them are the corrupt marriages (al-manakih al-fasidah), and what is hidden is pure fornication (al-zina al-sarih).

The second: the indecencies are all acts of disobedience (ma'asi), what is apparent of them are the deeds of the limbs (af'al al-jawarih), and what is hidden is the belief of the hearts (i'tiqad al-qulub).

﴿And sin and transgression without right﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: sin (al-ithm) is betrayal in matters, and transgression (al-baghy) is aggression against souls.

The second: sin (al-ithm) is wine, and transgression (al-baghy) is intoxication. The poet said:

I drank sin until my intellect went astray, and likewise sin takes away the intellects.

Wine was called "sin" (ithm), and intoxication was called "transgression" (baghy), because they arise from them both.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 34–36:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And for every nation there is a term﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: "And for every nation there is a Book (kitab) concerning what Allah has decreed for them of happiness or wretchedness, of punishment or mercy." This was said by Juwaybir.

The second: "And for every nation there is a prophet who calls them to His obedience and forbids them from disobeying Him." This was said by Mu'adh ibn Jabal.

The third: "For every nation there is a term concerning what Allah has ordained for them of life, and has decreed for them of death."

It may also bear a fourth meaning: "And for every nation there is a period during which they remain upon their religion, until they introduce disagreement into it."

﴿So when their term comes﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. One: the term of their death. The second: the term of their punishment, said by Juwaybir.

﴿They cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it﴾. This may bear two meanings. One: the term of their lives does not increase or decrease. The second: their punishment does not come earlier or later.(p-221)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 37:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Those will receive their portion of the Book﴾. Regarding this there are five interpretations:

The first: it is the punishment of Allah which He has prepared for those who associated partners with Him. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

The second: it is what has preceded for them of misery and happiness. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is their portion of their Book, which We wrote for them or against them according to their deeds which they did in the world, of good or evil. This was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: it is their portion of what was written for them of lifespan, provision and deeds. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: it is their portion of what they were promised in the Book of good or evil. This was said by al-Dahhak.

﴿Until when Our messengers come to them, causing them to die﴾. Regarding the causing to die of the messengers here there are two views:

One of them: it is the death of the world, at which the angels rebuke them.

The second: it is the death of being gathered to the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 38–39:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Until, when they have overtaken one another therein all together﴾ means: in the Fire, some of them catch up with others until they are all gathered together in it.

(p-222) ﴿The last of them will say to the first of them﴾ means: the followers, to the leaders, because by following them they are later than them. Likewise, in entering the Fire, the leaders precede the followers.

﴿Our Lord, these led us astray, so give them a double punishment of the Fire﴾ means: by one of the two doublings he intends their punishment for disbelief, and by the other, their punishment for misguiding.

This statement from the followers may carry two meanings. The first: lightening the punishment upon them. The second: taking vengeance upon the leaders by doubling the punishment on them.

So God answered them, saying: ﴿For each there is double﴾, meaning that although the leaders have a double punishment, because one of them is for disbelief and the other for misguiding, you, O followers, also have a double punishment. This is the view of the majority, and doubling a thing is an increase by its like.

There is a second opinion on this, reported by Mujahid: that "ḍi'f" (doubling) is among the names of punishment.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 38–39:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Until, when they have overtaken one another therein all together﴾ means: in the Fire, some of them catch up with others until they are all gathered together in it.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 40–41:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾. On this there are five opinions:

First: meaning, the gates will not be opened for their spirits, because they are opened for the spirit of the disbeliever and opened for the spirit of the believer. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

Second: they will not be opened for their supplication. This was said by al-Hasan.

Third: they will not be opened for their deeds. This was said by Mujahid and Ibrahim.

Fourth: the gates of heaven will not be opened for them for entry into Paradise, because Paradise is in heaven. This is the view of some of the later scholars.

Fifth: the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, so that mercy does not descend upon them. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

(p-223) ﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾. On this there are two opinions:

One: "the eye of the needle" is the hole of the needle. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrima, and al-Suddi.

The second: "the eye of the needle" is the deadly poison that enters the pores of the body, meaning its opening.

Regarding ﴿al-jamal﴾ (the camel) there are two readings (qira'at). The first, which is the reading of the majority, is al-jamal, with a fatha on the jim and a light mim, and it is the animal with four legs.

The second is al-jummal, with a damma on the jim and a shadda on the mim, and it is the thick rope (al-qals al-ghalizh). This is the reading of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and one of the two readings of Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas used to interpret it as the cable of the ship.

The meaning of the statement is that they will never enter Paradise, just as the camel will never enter the eye of the needle. Striking this example is more emphatic in despairing them than sending the statement unqualified in negation, and the Arabs use this for emphasis. The poet said:

When the crow turns white, I come to my family,
and pitch returns like fresh milk.

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying: ﴿For them from Hell will be a bed (mihad)﴾. al-Hasan said: a bed of fire. al-Mihad is the spread, and from it is taken the cradle (mahd) of the child.

﴿And above them will be coverings (ghawashin)﴾. On this there are three aspects:

First: that they are the quilts.

Second: that they are the clothing.

Third: that they are the canopies. This was said by al-Hasan.

(p-224) The intended meaning of this is that the fire is above them and beneath them, so He expressed what is beneath them by "mihad" and what is above them by "ghawashin".

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 42–43:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations. The first: the desires (al-ahwa') and innovations (al-bida'), said by Sahl ibn Abd Allah.

The second: mutual hatred and envy.

The third: malice (al-hiqd).

The fourth: He removed from their souls the wish for what belongs to others.

Concerning the removal (naza') there are two views. The first: God removed that from their breasts by His kindness (lutf).

The second: that the faith to which He guided them is what removed it from their breasts.

Concerning this resentment (ghill) there are two views. The first: that it is the resentment of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance), said by al-Hasan.

The second: that they do not bear enmity toward one another nor harbor malice after faith. It has been related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "I truly hope that I, Uthman, Talha and al-Zubayr are among those of whom Allah said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾." (p-225) It was also said that it was revealed concerning the people of Badr.

His saying, ﴿And they will say: All praise is due to Allah, who has guided us to this﴾, may have two meanings. The first: He guided us to removing resentment from our breasts. The second: He guided us to the firmness of faith in our hearts, such that He removed resentment from our breasts.

There is also a third interpretation. Juwaybir said: "He guided us to crossing the Sirat (the bridge over Hell) and entering Paradise."

قَوْلُهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ: ﴿وَعَلَى الأَعْرافِ رِجالٌ يَعْرِفُونَ كُلًّا بِسِيماهُمْ﴾ [And upon the A'raf (the heights) are men who recognize each by their marks]. أمّا الأعْرافُ فَسُورٌ بَيْنَ الجَنَّةِ والنّارِ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ، والسُّدِّيُّ، وهو جَمْعٌ واحِدُهُ عُرْفٌ وهو ما ارْتَفَعَ عَنْ غَيْرِهِ، ومِنهُ عُرْفُ الدِّيكِ وعُرْفُ الفَرَسِ، قالَ الرّاجِزُ:

؎ كُلُّ كِتابٍ لِجَمْعِهِ مُوافِي ∗∗∗ كالعِلْمِ المُوفِي عَلى الأعْرافِ.

[Every book, for gathering it, is a meeting-point, like knowledge that rises high above the heights.]

وَفِي الَّذِينَ عَلى الأعْرافِ خَمْسَةُ أقاوِيلَ: أحَدُها: أنَّهم فُضَلاءُ المُؤْمِنِينَ وعُلَماؤُهم، قالَهُ الحَسَنُ، ومُجاهِدٌ، قالَ أُمَيَّةُ بْنُ أبِي الصَّلْتِ:

؎ وآخَرُونَ عَلى الأعْرافِ قَدْ طَمِعُوا ∗∗∗ بِجَنَّةٍ حَفَّها الرُّمّانُ والخُضَرُ

[And others upon the heights have hoped for a Garden encircled by pomegranates and greenery.]

(p-٢٢٦)وَهَذا وإنْ كانَ شِعْرًا جاهِلِيًّا وحالُ الأعْرافِ مَنقُولٌ عَنْ خَبَرٍ يُرْوى فَيَحْتَمِلُ أمْرَيْنِ: أحَدُهُما: أنْ يَكُونَ أُمَيَّةُ قَدْ وصَلَ إلى عِلْمِهِ مِنَ الصُّحُفِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ.

والثّانِي: أنْ يَكُونَ اللَّهُ قَدْ أنْطَقَ بِهِ أُمَيَّةَ إلْهامًا لِتَصْدِيقِ ما جاءَ بِهِ القُرْآنُ.

والثّانِي: أنَّهم مَلائِكَةٌ يُرَوْنَ في صُوَرِ الرِّجالِ، قالَهُ أبُو مِجْلَزٍ.

والثّالِثُ: أنَّهم قَوْمٌ بَطَّأتْ بِهِمْ صَغائِرُهم إلى آخِرِ النّاسِ، قالَهُ حُذَيْفَةُ.

والرّابِعُ: أنَّهُ قَوْمٌ اسْتَوَتْ حَسَناتُهم وسَيِّئاتُهم فَجُعِلُوا هُنالِكَ حَتّى يَقْضِيَ اللَّهُ مِن أمْرِهِمْ ما يَشاءُ ثُمَّ يُدْخِلُهُمُ الجَنَّةَ، قالَهُ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ.

ومَعْنى قَوْلِهِ: ﴿يَعْرِفُونَ كُلًّا بِسِيماهُمْ﴾ يَعْنِي يَعْرِفُونَ أهْلَ النّارِ وأهْلَ الجَنَّةِ بِعَلامَتِهِمُ الَّتِي يَتَمَيَّزُونَ بِها، وعَلامَتُهم في وُجُوهِهِمْ وأعْيُنِهِمْ، قالَ الحَسَنُ البَصْرِيُّ: عَلامَةُ أهْلِ النّارِ سَوادُ الوُجُوهِ وزُرْقَةُ العُيُونِ، وعَلامَةُ أهْلِ الجَنَّةِ بَياضُ الوُجُوهِ وحُسْنُ العُيُونِ.

فَإنْ قِيلَ في أصْحابِ الأعْرافِ: إنَّهم فُضَلاءُ المُؤْمِنِينَ كانَ ذَلِكَ زِيادَةً في ثَوابِهِمْ ومُبالَغَةً في كَرامَتِهِمْ لِأنَّهم يَرَوْنَ مَنازِلَهم في الجَنَّةِ فَيَسْتَمْتِعُونَ بِها، ويَرَوْنَ عَذابَ النّارِ فَيَفْرَحُونَ بِالخَلاصِ مِنها.

(p-٢٢٧)وَإنْ قِيلَ: إنَّهُمُ المُفَضَّلُونَ وأصْحابُ الصَّغائِرِ مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ كانَ ذَلِكَ لِنَقْصِ ثَوابِهِمْ عَنِ اسْتِحْقاقِ الدُّخُولِ لِلْجَنَّةِ.

وَإنْ قِيلَ: إنَّهُمُ المَلائِكَةُ، احْتَمَلَ أمْرُهم ثَلاثَةَ أوْجُهٍ: أحَدُها: أنْ يُؤْمَرُوا بِذَلِكَ حَمْدًا لِأهْلِ الجَنَّةِ وذَمًّا لِأهْلِ النّارِ وزِيادَةً في الثَّوابِ والعِقابِ.

والثّانِي: أنْ يَكُونُوا حَفَظَةَ الأعْمالِ في الدُّنْيا الشّاهِدِينَ بِها عِنْدَ اللَّهِ في الآخِرَةِ أُمِرُوا بِذَلِكَ، ما أدَّوْهُ مِنَ الشَّهادَةِ تَبْشِيرًا لِأهْلِ الجَنَّةِ وتَوْبِيخًا لِأهْلِ النّارِ.

والثّالِثُ: أنْ يَكُونُوا خَزَنَةَ الجَنَّةِ والنّارِ، فَإنَّ مِنَ المَلائِكَةِ مَن أُفْرِدَ لِخَزَنَةِ الجَنَّةِ، ومِنهم مَن أُفْرِدَ لِخَزَنَةِ النّارِ، ويَكُونُ هَؤُلاءِ قَدْ جُمِعَ لَهم بَيْنَ الأمْرَيْنِ، واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ بِغَيْبِ ذَلِكَ.

وَحَكى ابْنُ الأنْبارِيِّ أنَّ قَوْلَهُ: ﴿وَعَلَى الأَعْرافِ رِجالٌ﴾ مَعْناهُ عَلى مَعْرِفَةِ أهْلِ الجَنَّةِ والنّارِ رِجالٌ، وأنَّ قَوْلَهُ: ﴿ادْخُلُوا الجَنَّةَ لا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [Enter Paradise; no fear shall be upon you] الآيَةَ مِن قَوْلِ أصْحابِ الأعْرافِ، وهو مُخالِفٌ لِقَوْلِ جَمِيعِ المُفَسِّرِينَ.

قَوْلُهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ: ﴿وَعَلَى الأَعْرافِ رِجالٌ يَعْرِفُونَ كُلًّا بِسِيماهُمْ﴾ [And upon the A'raf (the heights) are men who recognize each by their marks]. أمّا الأعْرافُ فَسُورٌ بَيْنَ الجَنَّةِ والنّارِ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ، والسُّدِّيُّ، وهو جَمْعٌ واحِدُهُ عُرْفٌ وهو ما ارْتَفَعَ عَنْ غَيْرِهِ، ومِنهُ عُرْفُ الدِّيكِ وعُرْفُ الفَرَسِ، قالَ الرّاجِزُ:

؎ كُلُّ كِتابٍ لِجَمْعِهِ مُوافِي ∗∗∗ كالعِلْمِ المُوفِي عَلى الأعْرافِ.

[Every book, for gathering it, is a meeting-point, like knowledge that rises high above the heights.]

وَفِي الَّذِينَ عَلى الأعْرافِ خَمْسَةُ أقاوِيلَ: أحَدُها: أنَّهم فُضَلاءُ المُؤْمِنِينَ وعُلَماؤُهم، قالَهُ الحَسَنُ، ومُجاهِدٌ، قالَ أُمَيَّةُ بْنُ أبِي الصَّلْتِ:

؎ وآخَرُونَ عَلى الأعْرافِ قَدْ طَمِعُوا ∗∗∗ بِجَنَّةٍ حَفَّها الرُّمّانُ والخُضَرُ

[And others upon the heights have hoped for a Garden encircled by pomegranates and greenery.]

In His words ﴿And they will call out﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: it means "will call out" (yunadi), since it refers to the future. The second: it is elided, and its implied sense is: when the Day of Resurrection comes, the people of the heights (ashab al-A'raf) will call out.

(p-228) His words, mighty and majestic be He: ﴿Pour out upon us some of the water or of what God has provided you﴾. There are two interpretations of this:

First: "some of the water" means the water of mercy, and "what God has provided you" means nearness (to Him, through acts of worship).

Second: "some of the water" means the water of life, and "what God has provided you" means blessings.

And the words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book﴾ — meaning the Qur'an.

﴿We had explained it upon knowledge﴾ — concerning this there are two views. The first: We clarified in it what is permissible and what is forbidden, upon knowledge of what is in the interest (maslahah) [of the creatures].

The second: We distinguished through it guidance from misguidance, upon knowledge of the reward and the punishment.

﴿As guidance and mercy﴾ — this may carry two meanings. The first: that guidance (huda) is proof (burhan).

The second: that guidance is direction (irshad), and mercy is subtle kindness (lutf).

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿Do they await anything but its final outcome?﴾ — that is, do they await anything? Here waiting is expressed by the term "looking" (nazar). ﴿But its final outcome﴾ — that is, the ta'wil (final outcome/interpretation) of the Qur'an. Concerning this there are two views. The first: its consequence in terms of recompense, as said by al-Hasan.

The second: what it contains of resurrection, rising again, and reckoning.

﴿On the day its final outcome comes﴾ — concerning this there are two views. The first: the judgment according to it, as said by al-Hasan.

The second: the consequence of what Allah promised them in this world and the Hereafter, as said by al-Kalbi.

﴿Those who had forgotten it before will say﴾ — concerning this there are two statements. The first: the meaning of "forgotten it" is that they turned away from it, so it became like the forgotten, as said by Abu Mijlaz.

The second: the angels at the time of visible witnessing, with what they gave them good news of, of reward and punishment.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 54:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾. Regarding the omission of hastening the creation of them in the least amount of time, although He is capable of that, there are four aspects. The first: that bringing them into being thing after thing and state after state is more eloquent in wisdom and more indicative of the soundness of management, so that with the passing of times, by what He brings into being of creatures, there is a repeated affirmation that He is Knowing and Capable, who directs affairs according to His choice and runs them according to His will.

The second: that this is in consideration of the angels, He created one thing after another.

The third: that this was arranged according to the days: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, and these are six days, so He brought forth creation in them. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: so that He may teach us by this the whole of calculation from six, and from it branches out all the rest of the numbers. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿Then He istawa over the Throne﴾. Concerning this there are two statements. The first: its meaning is that His command istawa over the Throne. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: He seized control (istawla) over the Throne, as the poet said:

"Bishr has seized control over Iraq, without sword or spilled blood."

Regarding "the Throne" there are three sayings. The first: it is sovereignty, referred to by the Throne and the couch, in accordance with the custom of the kings of the earth in sitting upon thrones. This was related by Ibn Bahr.

The second: it is all the heavens, because they are a canopy, and every canopy in the Arabic language is a throne. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿fallen upon its trellises﴾ [al-Kahf: 42] [al-Hajj: 45], meaning upon its roofs.

The third: it is a place in the heaven, at its highest and most noble part, veiled from the angels of the heaven.

﴿He covers the night with the day﴾, meaning He covers the darkness of the night with the light of the day.

﴿Seeking it urgently﴾, because the swiftness of the succession of night and day makes each of them like one seeking the other.

﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars [are] subjected by His command﴾ admits of two aspects. The first: made subservient by His power. The second: running by His decree.

﴿Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command﴾ admits of two aspects. The first: that He is the owner of the creation and its management. The second: to Him is their return, and upon Him is their recompense.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 55–56:

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: it refers to desire and fear, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

(p-231) The second: tadarru' (tadarru') is humility and submission, and khufyah (khufyah) is sincerity of the heart.

It is also possible that tadarru' is with the body, and khufyah is sincerity of the heart.

﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾, meaning in supplication. I'tida' (i'tida', transgression) in this regard has three opinions. The first: that one asks for what one does not deserve of the ranks of the Prophets, as said by Abu Mijlaz.

The second: that one supplicates for curse and destruction upon those who do not deserve it, as said by Muqatil.

The third: that one raises one's voice in supplication. Abu ʿUthman al-Nahdi narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: "We were with the Prophet ﷺ on a military campaign, and they came upon a valley, and the people began to glorify God, declare His oneness, and raise their voices. The Prophet ﷺ said: (O people, be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent; you are calling upon One who is All-Hearing, Near, and He is with you)."

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions. The first: do not corrupt it through disbelief after its reformation through faith.

The second: do not corrupt it through injustice after its reformation through justice.

The third: do not corrupt it through disobedience after its reformation through obedience, as said by al-Kalbi.

The fourth: do not corrupt it by killing a believer after its reformation by his remaining alive, as said by al-Hasan.

﴿And call upon Him in fear and hope﴾. It may have two meanings. The first: fear of His punishment and hope for His reward.

The second: fear of rejection and hope for acceptance.

﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾. If it is asked: why did he drop the ta' marbuta from qarib (qarib) when mercy (rahmah) is feminine? To this there are two answers.

The first: that mercy from Allah is a bestowal from Him, so it was made masculine according to the meaning, which is that Allah's bestowal is near to the doers of good, as said by al-Akhfash.

(p-232) The second: that what is meant by it is the place of mercy, as said by al-Farra', as the poet ʿUrwah ibn Hizam said:

؎ In the evening, ʿAfra' is neither near to you, so as to draw close, nor is ʿAfra' far from you.

He intended by "far" its place, so he dropped the ta' marbuta, and he intended by "near" her herself, so he kept the ta' marbuta.

"The Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿And the good land—its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾, meaning: the land of good soil.

﴿Its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾, meaning: its vegetation comes forth good and excellent.

﴿But that which is bad does not come forth except meagerly﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: that the *nakid* (meagre) is what is little and of no benefit; this was said by al-Suddi.

The second: that it is hardship in its severity, which prevents good from it. The poet said:

؎ Give what you have given as good, for there is no good in the miserly and the grudging

This is a parable that Allah the Exalted struck for the believer and the disbeliever: the believer is made like the good land, and the disbeliever like the bad, salty (*sabkha*) land. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Suddi."

The second: the breadth of the body and the length of the frame. It has been said that the shortest of them in height was twelve cubits.

﴿So remember the bounties of Allah﴾: its meaning is the blessings of Allah. The poet said:

؎ A white man who does not dread poverty, nor sever kinship, nor betray a covenant..."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 70–72:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: Indeed there has fallen upon you from your Lord abomination (rijs) and wrath﴾. Regarding ar-rijs (abomination/uncleanness) there are three opinions. The first: it is the punishment; this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The second: it is the anger (al-sukhṭ); this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: ar-rijs and ar-rijz (both meaning the same thing), except that the zāy was changed into sīn, just as the sīn was changed into tāʾ in the saying of the poet:

Ala laḥā Allāhu Banī as-Saʿlāh, ʿAmr ibn Yarbūʿ, liʾāma an-nāt (May God curse the Banu as-Saʿlah, ʿAmr ibn Yarbuʿ, the base of people).

Laysū bi-aʿfāf wa-lā akyāt (They are not chaste, nor are they shrewd).

He means an-nās (the people), and akyās (shrewd ones).

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿concerning names you have named﴾, meaning the idols. Regarding the meaning of their naming, there are two views. The first: in naming them gods which they worship. The second: their naming of some of them, that it gives them rain, and another that it brings them provision, another that it heals the sick, and another that it accompanies them on journeys.

It is said: Hud only commanded them to worship God alone and to refrain from wronging people, but they refused and said: "Who is mightier than us in strength?" So they were destroyed.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on Surah 7, verses 73–78:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿This is God's she-camel, a sign for you﴾. Regarding the word *āyah* (sign) here, there are two interpretations. The first is that *āyah* means *al-farḍ* (an obligation), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent down therein verses﴾ [al-Nur: 1], meaning obligations. The meaning of the statement would then be: "This is God's she-camel, and it is an obligation upon you that you leave her alone ﴿to feed on God's earth, and do not touch her with harm﴾," meaning do not hamstring her.

The second is that it is the sign that indicates His power.

The sign in it consists of two signs. The first is that she came out of a smooth rock, which labored with her as a woman labors in childbirth, and then it split open to produce her in the form they had demanded.

The second is that she had a day of water, and they had a day of water reserved for them, on which she did not approach their water. This is related from Abu al-Tufayl, al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And He settled you in the earth﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first is that He made you dwell in the land, which is the land of al-Hijr between Syria and Medina.

The second is that in it there are dwellings to which you return. From this is the saying of the Arabs: *bawwa'tuhu manzilan* (I gave him a dwelling), when you enable him to occupy it so that he may take shelter in it. The poet said:

*He was settled in the midst of his people, and his dwelling was completed among his folk.*

(p-236) That is, he was given a place of honor in the pure lineage.

﴿You take from its plains palaces﴾. *Qusur* (palaces) are the structures that are built high among dwellings. They took them in the plains of the earth so that they might spend the summer in them.

﴿And you hew out the mountains as houses﴾, so that they might be their dwellings in winter, because they are more secure, more lasting and warmer. Thus they were long in hopes and long in lifespans.

﴿So remember the bounties of God﴾. Regarding this, what we have already mentioned applies, that is, His blessings or His covenants.

﴿And do not go about in the earth causing corruption﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first is: do not commit acts of disobedience in it.

The second is: do not call to the worship of other than God.

Regarding *al-'athw* (mischief), there are two interpretations. The first is that it is striving in falsehood.

The second is that it is an act that brings harm upon its doer.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾. Regarding *al-rajfah* (the earthquake) there are three opinions. The first is that it is the movement of the earth, which shook beneath them.

The second is that it is the shout (*al-ṣayḥah*), as said by Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The third is that it is a tremor by which they were destroyed, as said by Ibn Abbas.

﴿So they were in their abode, lying prostrate﴾. Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Suddi said: Whatever is in the Qur'an as ﴿their abode (dar)﴾ means by it their city, and whatever is in it as ﴿their abodes (diyar)﴾ means by it their dwellings. Regarding *al-jathim* (lying prostrate) there are two opinions. The first is that it refers to one kneeling upon his knees, because they became dead in this state.

The second is that its meaning is that they became in the morning like ash lying prostrate, because the thunderbolt burned them.

It was also said that it happened after the afternoon.

﴿So he turned away from them﴾, that is, he went out from among them. It was said that Salih went out from them to Ramla in Palestine with those of his people who believed with him, and they were one hundred and ten. It was also said that no nation perished while its prophet was among it.

﴿So We saved him and his family﴾. In this there are two views. The first: We delivered him (fa-khallasnāhu).

؎ Muhammad has not ceased, since God forgave him, [to remember] what passed and what remained (fa-mā wanā Muḥammadun mudh an ghafara lahu al-ilāhu mā maḍā wa-mā ghabar)

(p-238) The second: [she was] among those who remained behind in deliverance, from the expression "fulān ghabara ʿannā zamānan" (so-and-so was absent from us for a time) when he was absent. The poet said:

؎ Is it after us, or after them, that salvation is hoped for our remaining ones? (afa-baʿdanā aw baʿdahum * yurjā li-ghābirinā al-falāḥ)

The third: [she was] among those who remained behind in grief, because she met the destruction of her people. This was said by Abu ʿUbayda.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 85–87:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And do not sit at every path, threatening⦗and⦘ ...﴾. Al-Sirat (ṣirāṭ): the road. The poet said:

؎ We filled their land with horses until we left them more humbled than the road.

Regarding the intended meaning of it, there are three opinions. The first: they used to sit on the road to Shu'ayb, harming whoever came to him seeking to believe in him, and threatening him with killing. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada.

The second: that he forbade them from highway robbery. This was said by Abu Hurayra.

The third: that they were the tax collectors, and he forbade them from levying taxes on people's property.

(p-239) ﴿and barring from the way of Allah those who believe in Him﴾. It may bear two meanings. The first: you bar the believers from obeying Allah and worshipping Him. The second: you bar those who wish to believe by seducing and deceiving them.

﴿and seeking to make it crooked﴾. Qatada said: meaning, you seek the way to be crooked away from the truth.

The difference between ʿiwaj (with a kasra on the ʿayn) and ʿawaj (with a fatha on the ʿayn) is that ʿiwaj with a kasra refers to what is in religion and is not seen, while ʿawaj with a fatha refers to what is in a piece of wood and is seen.

﴿And remember when you were few, and He multiplied you﴾. Al-Zajjaj related three aspects regarding it: the first: your number increased after being few. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is because Madyan ibn Ibrahim married Zina, the daughter of Lut, and the people of Madyan descended from her.

The second: He multiplied you in wealth after poverty.

The third: He multiplied you in strength after weakness.

Some exegetes mentioned a fourth aspect: that He multiplied them by lengthening their lifespans after they had been shortened before.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 88–89:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your millah (religion/community) after Allah has saved us from it﴾. The difference between al-millah (the religious path, community) and al-din (religion) is that al-millah is what Allah has legislated, while al-din is what people believe in seeking nearness to Allah. Thus every din is a millah, but not every millah is a din.

If it is said: "Returning to a thing" means going back to it after having come out of it. Was Shu'ayb then on the millah of his people in disbelief, such that he would say: ﴿if we return to your millah﴾? In answer to this there are three aspects: (p-240) The first: this is a report about those who followed Shu'ayb from among his people, who had been on the millah of disbelief before following him.

The second: he said this on the assumption that, if he were upon it, he would not have returned to it.

The third: the mention of "return" is used of one who initiates an act even if he had not previously done the like of it, as in the saying of people: "Harm has returned to me from so-and-so," even though he had not previously inflicted the like upon them, as in the verse of the poet:

"If the days were once kind to me,
then sins have returned to them (the days)...
Something of sweet life came to me, I found it bitter,
distress upon distress following its traces."

Then he said: ﴿And it is not for us to return to it, except that Allah, our Lord, should will it﴾. Concerning this there are two views: The first: that we would return to the town, except that Allah wills it; this was said by some of the theologians.

The second, which is the view of the majority: that we would return to the millah of disbelief and the worship of idols.

If it is said: Allah the Exalted does not will the worship of idols, so what is the sense of this statement from Shu'ayb? The answer to this has three aspects: The first: that among their millah there was what it is permissible to worship by.

The second: that if He willed the worship of an idol, its worship would be obedience, since He willed it, just as devotion through venerating the Black Stone.

The third: that this statement of Shu'ayb is by way of impossibility and refusal, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40], and like the saying of people: "until the crow turns white."

Then he said: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of those who decide﴾. Concerning this there are two aspects: The first: "reveal (uncover) between us and our people," said by Qatadah.

The second: "judge between us and our people with truth, and You are the best of judges."

Al-Farra' mentioned that the people of Oman call the judge "al-fatih" and "al-fattah."

Others said: it is the dialect of Murad. The poet said:

"Oh, convey to the Banu 'Usam a message,
that I am independent of your fattah (judge)."

(p-241) Ibn 'Abbas said: "I did not know the meaning of His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of those who decide﴾ until I heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan say: 'Come, let me fatihuki (decide between us),' meaning: let me judge you."

It was also said: he was named so because He opens the door of knowledge that has been closed to others.

If it is said: What is the meaning of His saying "in truth," since it is known that Allah does not judge except in truth? The answer to this has four aspects: The first: he said this as a description of His judgment, not as a request for it.

The second: he asked Allah to reveal to his opponents among his people that he was upon the truth.

The third: its meaning is "judge between us with what is the truth," said by Ibn Bahr.

The fourth: "judge in this world by granting victory to the truth," said by al-Suddi.
