Then he said: ﴿And it is not for us to return to it, except that Allah, our Lord, should will it﴾. Concerning this there are two views: The first: that we would return to the town, except that Allah wills it; this was said by some of the theologians.

The second, which is the view of the majority: that we would return to the millah of disbelief and the worship of idols.

If it is said: Allah the Exalted does not will the worship of idols, so what is the sense of this statement from Shu'ayb? The answer to this has three aspects: The first: that among their millah there was what it is permissible to worship by.

The second: that if He willed the worship of an idol, its worship would be obedience, since He willed it, just as devotion through venerating the Black Stone.

The third: that this statement of Shu'ayb is by way of impossibility and refusal, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40], and like the saying of people: "until the crow turns white."

Then he said: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of those who decide﴾. Concerning this there are two aspects: The first: "reveal (uncover) between us and our people," said by Qatadah.

The second: "judge between us and our people with truth, and You are the best of judges."

Al-Farra' mentioned that the people of Oman call the judge "al-fatih" and "al-fattah."

Others said: it is the dialect of Murad. The poet said:

"Oh, convey to the Banu 'Usam a message,
that I am independent of your fattah (judge)."

(p-241) Ibn 'Abbas said: "I did not know the meaning of His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of those who decide﴾ until I heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan say: 'Come, let me fatihuki (decide between us),' meaning: let me judge you."

It was also said: he was named so because He opens the door of knowledge that has been closed to others.

If it is said: What is the meaning of His saying "in truth," since it is known that Allah does not judge except in truth? The answer to this has four aspects: The first: he said this as a description of His judgment, not as a request for it.

The second: he asked Allah to reveal to his opponents among his people that he was upon the truth.

The third: its meaning is "judge between us with what is the truth," said by Ibn Bahr.

The fourth: "judge in this world by granting victory to the truth," said by al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 90–92:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, it was as if they had never dwelt therein﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations:

First: "as if they had never remained therein" (ka-an lam yuqimu fiha), said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Second: "as if they had never lived therein" (ka-an lam ya'ishu fiha), said by al-Akhfash.

Third: "as if they had never enjoyed comfort therein" (ka-an lam yan'amu fiha), said by Qatadah.

Fourth: "as if they had never prospered therein" (ka-an lam yu'ammaru fiha), said by Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, they were the losers﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One: "with disbelief" (bil-kufr).

Second: "with destruction" (bil-halak), said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on verses 7:93–95:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We did not send to any town a prophet except that We seized its people with adversity and hardship﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions. The first: al-ba'sa' (adversity) is drought (qahṭ), and al-darra' (hardship) is illness and calamities. This is related from al-Hasan.

The second: al-ba'sa' is hunger, and al-darra' is poverty. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: al-ba'sa' is trial (balaʾ), and al-darra' is chronic affliction (zamana).

The fourth: al-ba'sa' is the hardship that befell them in their persons, and al-darra' is what befell them in their wealth. This is reported by 'Ali ibn 'Isa.

It may also admit a fifth opinion: that al-ba'sa' refers to wars.

﴿So that they might humble themselves﴾. Regarding this there are two meanings. One: they repent. The second: they supplicate. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Then We replaced the evil with good﴾. Regarding this there are two meanings. One: in place of hardship, ease (rakhaʾ). This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, and Mujahid.

The second: in place of good and evil.

﴿Until they multiplied﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions. The first: until they became numerous. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi. Labid said:

"And people, after slaughter, have multiplied, and many have departed from them and moved on."

The second: until they turned away. This is said by Ibn Bahr.

The third: until they were delighted. This is said by Qatada.

The fourth: until they grew fat. This is said by al-Hasan, and from it is the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Hazim:

"When he had multiplied and acquired wealth, he grew fat, turning away with an arrogant sideways glance."

(p-243) ﴿And they said: Indeed hardship and ease have touched our fathers﴾, meaning adversity and ease. They mean that adversity and hardship were not a punishment for your denial, but rather it is God's custom in His creation that after every season of abundance (khiṣb) there comes drought (jadb), and after every drought there comes abundance.

In his commentary on the words of the Most High, ﴿So they do not hear﴾, [it means] they do not accept, as He said in the prayer, "God hears whoever praises Him" (sami'a Allahu liman hamidah), meaning God accepts from whoever praises Him. And the poet said:

I called upon God until I feared that God would not hear what I say,

meaning, would not accept it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 101–102:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And We did not find in most of them any covenant﴾. Regarding His saying ﴿any covenant﴾ (min ʿahd), there are two opinions.

The first: that ʿahd (covenant) here means obedience, meaning: We did not find in most of them any obedience to their prophets, because He said after it: ﴿And indeed, We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾. In this interpretation, the min (from) in this place is redundant (zāʾidah).

The second: that it is to be understood in its apparent sense of covenant, i.e., any fulfilment of their covenant.

Regarding what is meant by ʿahd here, there are three opinions.

The first: the covenant (mīthāq) which God took from them in the loins of Adam. This was said by Abu Jaʿfar al-Tabari.

The second: what God placed in their intellects of the obligation to be grateful for blessings, and that God is the Bestower of blessings. This was said by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

The third: that it is what He enjoined upon them through the prophets, that they should worship Him and not associate anything with Him. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿And indeed, We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾. Regarding His saying ﴿defiantly disobedient﴾ (fāsiqīn), there are two aspects. The first: departing from His obedience.

The second: being treacherous regarding His covenant. This indicates that the disobedient (ʿuṣāt) are more numerous than the obedient (muṭīʿīn).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 103–108:

(p-245) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is fitting for me that I should not say about God except the truth﴾. In ﴿fitting (ḥaqīq)﴾ there are two meanings. One of them: eager (ḥarīṣ), as said by Abu ʿUbayda.

(p-246) His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿And We revealed to Moses, "Throw down your staff."﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: The staff was the first of Moses's signs, and it was from the myrtle (ās) of Paradise. Its length was ten cubits, matching Moses's own height. He approached the gate of Pharaoh, and it cast terror upon him. Pharaoh then grew white-haired, and out of shame before his people he dyed his hair black. Thus Pharaoh was the first to dye with black.

﴿Then behold, it swallowed up﴾ The meaning of talqaf (swallows up) is quick seizing, except that what is intended here is the swift swallowing of it with the mouth.

Abu Hatim said: In some readings it is read as talqqam, with a meem and with shadda (emphasis on the letter). The poet said:

"You are the staff of Moses, which has never ceased to swallow up what the sorcerer fabricates."

As for His saying: ﴿what they fabricate﴾, there are two explanations. The first: its meaning is "they reverse/turn about," from which comes al-mu'tafikat (the overturned cities), that is, the overturned ones. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

The second: its meaning is "they lie," because al-ifk is falsehood. This was said by Mujahid.

If it is asked: Why did Moses order the sorcerers to cast down, when that is disbelief on their part, and a prophet may not order such a thing? It is answered that there are two responses to this.

The first: the content of his command is, "If you are truthful, then cast down."

The second: the statement is taken according to what is sound and permissible, not according to what is corrupt and impossible.

His saying: ﴿So the truth came to pass﴾ means the truth became manifest. This was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid. Regarding the truth that became manifest, there are two views. The first: the staff of Moses prevailed over the ropes of the sorcerers. The second: the prophethood of Moses became manifest over the lordship (rububiyyah, the claim to divine lordship) of Pharaoh.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿And the sorcerers were cast down prostrate﴾ Concerning their prostration there are two views. The first: they prostrated to Moses, submitting to him and believing in him. The second: they prostrated to God, affirming His lordship, because they ﴿said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron."﴾ Concerning their prostration there are two views. The first: God inspired them to do so as a kindness (lutf, divine grace that brings a person closer to obedience) toward them. The second: Moses and Aaron prostrated in thanks to God when the truth prevailed over falsehood, so they followed them in prostrating to God in obedience.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 123–129:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the chiefs of Pharaoh's people said﴾, to the end of the verse. ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people﴾ has three interpretations. The first: they are its nobles. The second: they are its leaders. The third: they are the small group and the handful of people who believed along with them.

The difference between *al-rahṭ* (a group) and *al-nafar* (a few men) is in two respects. The first: *al-rahṭ* is more numerous and *al-nafar* is fewer. The second: *al-rahṭ* is stronger and *al-nafar* is weaker.

As for calling them *al-malaʾ* (the chiefs), there are two explanations. The first: they are "fulfilled" (*maliʾūn*) by what is required of them. The second: because their awe fills the souls.

There is a third explanation: because they fill the chests of the assemblies.

If it is asked: what is the reason for their boldness in denouncing Pharaoh, given that they worship him? It is said: (p. 248) because they saw from him a departure from his custom and the custom of kings in striking down those who openly oppose and defy them. That was part of God's gentleness toward Moses.

As for His saying ﴿to make corruption in the land﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: to make corruption in it by worshipping other than you and calling to a religion other than yours. The second: to make corruption in it by overpowering it and seizing it from his people.

Then they said ﴿and abandon you and your gods﴾. If it is asked: what is the reason for their saying this to him, when they had affirmed him in his saying ﴿I am your lord, the most high﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24]? The answer to this is given in three ways. The first: he used to worship idols, and his people used to worship him. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: he used to worship what is considered beautiful among cattle, and for this reason al-Samiri produced a calf, a body that had a lowing sound, and said, "This is your god and the god of Moses." He was worshipped among his people. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: they were idols which his people worshipped in order to draw near to him. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Ibn Abbas read ﴿wa-yadharaka wa-ilahatak﴾, meaning "and your worship."

Al-Hasan said: Pharaoh used to worship and be worshipped.

According to this reading, the question falls away.

Ibn Qutayba mentioned a second interpretation of this reading: that *al-ilaha* is the sun, and the Arabs call the sun *al-ilaha*. He cited the verse of al-A'sha:

"I did not mention the terror until I departed, shortly before the sun, from it, nearby."

He means the sun. So the interpretation of the verse becomes: "and abandon you and the sun, until you worship." According to this, the question directed at it is what preceded.

﴿He said: We will kill their sons and spare their women﴾. He turned from killing Moses to killing the sons only because he knew that he could not kill Moses, either because of Moses' strength or because he imagined that Moses was protected from being killed. So he turned to killing the sons, to uproot the people of Moses from the Children of Israel, so that they would be weakened against Pharaoh. ﴿And we will spare their women﴾: concerning this there are two sayings. (p. 249) The first: that we will examine their wombs and see what children are in them. It is derived from *al-hayaʾ*, which is one of the names of the private part; this was related by Ibn Bahr.

The second, which is more apparent: its meaning is that we will keep them alive, because of their weakness in contending and their inability to fight.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Moses said to his people: Seek help in God and be patient﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: he commanded them with this to console them regarding Pharaoh's threat, just as one who has been struck by hardship says, "I have sought help in God."

The second: it is a promise from him that God will help them against Pharaoh if they seek help from Him.

Then he said ﴿and be patient﴾, which may have two meanings. The first: be patient in what you are in of hardship, hoping for God's reward. The second: he commanded them to be patient while awaiting God's victory.

﴿Indeed, the earth belongs to God; He gives it as an inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: he said this to console his people, that this world does not remain for anyone, so it will not remain for Pharaoh, because it passes from one people to another. The second: he informed them by this that God will give them the land of Pharaoh as an inheritance.

﴿And the final outcome is for the God-fearing﴾ may have two meanings. The first: he means in the Hereafter, through reward. The second: in this world, through victory.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us﴾. Concerning this there are four sayings. The first: the harm before and after was the imposition of the jizya (poll tax). This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: the harm before was their being made to labour for the Children of Israel in their work for half the day, and then being released for the rest of the day to earn for themselves. The harm after was their being made to labour the whole day without food or drink. This was said by Juwaybir.

The third: the harm that was before was enslavement and the killing of sons, and the harm that was after was the threat of renewing this against them. This was related by Ibn Isa.

(p. 250) The fourth: the harm that was before was that they used to strike the bricks and he would give them straw; the harm after was that they came to strike the bricks while he placed the straw upon them. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Concerning their saying ﴿before you came to us and after you came to us﴾ there are two sayings. The first: before you came to us with the message, and after you came to us with it. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: before you came to us with God's covenant to you that He would deliver us, and after you came to us with it.

In this saying of theirs there are two possibilities. The first: it is a complaint about what befell them from Pharaoh, and a seeking of help from Moses. The second: they said it as an expression of impatience with the promise of Moses. This was related by Ibn Isa.

﴿He said: It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾. *Asa* (it may be) in the language means hope and apprehension.

Al-Hasan said: *asa* from God is binding. Al-Zajjaj said: *asa* from God is certainty.

﴿and will make you successors in the land, and will see how you act﴾. In His saying ﴿will see﴾ there are two meanings. The first: "will see." The second: "will know." In Moses' saying this to his people there are two matters. The first: the promise of victory and of succession in the land. The second: a warning against corruption in it, because God, exalted is He, sees how they act.

In Moses' saying this to his people there are two matters. The first: the promise of victory and of succession in the land. The second: a warning against corruption in it, because God, exalted is He, sees how they act.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 123–129:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the chiefs of Pharaoh's people said﴾, to the end of the verse. ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people﴾ has three interpretations. The first: they are its nobles. The second: they are its leaders. The third: they are the small group and the handful of people who believed along with them.

The difference between *al-rahṭ* (a group) and *al-nafar* (a few men) is in two respects. The first: *al-rahṭ* is more numerous and *al-nafar* is fewer. The second: *al-rahṭ* is stronger and *al-nafar* is weaker.

As for calling them *al-malaʾ* (the chiefs), there are two explanations. The first: they are "fulfilled" (*maliʾūn*) by what is required of them. The second: because their awe fills the souls.

There is a third explanation: because they fill the chests of the assemblies.

If it is asked: what is the reason for their boldness in denouncing Pharaoh, given that they worship him? It is said: (p. 248) because they saw from him a departure from his custom and the custom of kings in striking down those who openly oppose and defy them. That was part of God's gentleness toward Moses.

As for His saying ﴿to make corruption in the land﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: to make corruption in it by worshipping other than you and calling to a religion other than yours. The second: to make corruption in it by overpowering it and seizing it from his people.

Then they said ﴿and abandon you and your gods﴾. If it is asked: what is the reason for their saying this to him, when they had affirmed him in his saying ﴿I am your lord, the most high﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24]? The answer to this is given in three ways. The first: he used to worship idols, and his people used to worship him. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: he used to worship what is considered beautiful among cattle, and for this reason al-Samiri produced a calf, a body that had a lowing sound, and said, "This is your god and the god of Moses." He was worshipped among his people. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: they were idols which his people worshipped in order to draw near to him. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Ibn Abbas read ﴿wa-yadharaka wa-ilahatak﴾, meaning "and your worship."

Al-Hasan said: Pharaoh used to worship and be worshipped.

According to this reading, the question falls away.

Ibn Qutayba mentioned a second interpretation of this reading: that *al-ilaha* is the sun, and the Arabs call the sun *al-ilaha*. He cited the verse of al-A'sha:

"I did not mention the terror until I departed, shortly before the sun, from it, nearby."

He means the sun. So the interpretation of the verse becomes: "and abandon you and the sun, until you worship." According to this, the question directed at it is what preceded.

﴿He said: We will kill their sons and spare their women﴾. He turned from killing Moses to killing the sons only because he knew that he could not kill Moses, either because of Moses' strength or because he imagined that Moses was protected from being killed. So he turned to killing the sons, to uproot the people of Moses from the Children of Israel, so that they would be weakened against Pharaoh. ﴿And we will spare their women﴾: concerning this there are two sayings. (p. 249) The first: that we will examine their wombs and see what children are in them. It is derived from *al-hayaʾ*, which is one of the names of the private part; this was related by Ibn Bahr.

The second, which is more apparent: its meaning is that we will keep them alive, because of their weakness in contending and their inability to fight.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Moses said to his people: Seek help in God and be patient﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: he commanded them with this to console them regarding Pharaoh's threat, just as one who has been struck by hardship says, "I have sought help in God."

The second: it is a promise from him that God will help them against Pharaoh if they seek help from Him.

Then he said ﴿and be patient﴾, which may have two meanings. The first: be patient in what you are in of hardship, hoping for God's reward. The second: he commanded them to be patient while awaiting God's victory.

﴿Indeed, the earth belongs to God; He gives it as an inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: he said this to console his people, that this world does not remain for anyone, so it will not remain for Pharaoh, because it passes from one people to another. The second: he informed them by this that God will give them the land of Pharaoh as an inheritance.

﴿And the final outcome is for the God-fearing﴾ may have two meanings. The first: he means in the Hereafter, through reward. The second: in this world, through victory.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us﴾. Concerning this there are four sayings. The first: the harm before and after was the imposition of the jizya (poll tax). This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: the harm before was their being made to labour for the Children of Israel in their work for half the day, and then being released for the rest of the day to earn for themselves. The harm after was their being made to labour the whole day without food or drink. This was said by Juwaybir.

The third: the harm that was before was enslavement and the killing of sons, and the harm that was after was the threat of renewing this against them. This was related by Ibn Isa.

(p. 250) The fourth: the harm that was before was that they used to strike the bricks and he would give them straw; the harm after was that they came to strike the bricks while he placed the straw upon them. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Concerning their saying ﴿before you came to us and after you came to us﴾ there are two sayings. The first: before you came to us with the message, and after you came to us with it. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: before you came to us with God's covenant to you that He would deliver us, and after you came to us with it.

In this saying of theirs there are two possibilities. The first: it is a complaint about what befell them from Pharaoh, and a seeking of help from Moses. The second: they said it as an expression of impatience with the promise of Moses. This was related by Ibn Isa.

﴿He said: It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾. *Asa* (it may be) in the language means hope and apprehension.

Al-Hasan said: *asa* from God is binding. Al-Zajjaj said: *asa* from God is certainty.

﴿and will make you successors in the land, and will see how you act﴾. In His saying ﴿will see﴾ there are two meanings. The first: "will see." The second: "will know." The second: a warning against corruption in it, because God, exalted is He, sees how they act.

**The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-‘Uyun) on 7:130–131:**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought]﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first is that it means with hunger. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second is that the meaning of *al-sinin* (the years) is *al-judub* (barrenness, failed harvests). This was said by al-Hasan.

The Arabs say: *akhadhathhumu al-sanah* ("the drought seized them") when they suffered famine and their land became barren.

al-Farra’ said: The intended meaning of *al-sinin* is barrenness and dearth, year after year.

(p-251) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours by right." And if evil befell them, they ascribed it as an omen to Moses and those with him﴾. Concerning *al-hasanah* (good) and *al-sayyi'ah* (evil) here there are two views. The first is that *al-hasanah* is abundance and *al-sayyi'ah* is famine. The second is that *al-hasanah* is security and *al-sayyi'ah* is fear.

﴿They said, "This is ours"﴾, meaning: this was our condition in our homelands and before we followed you, out of their ignorance that Allah Most High is the one who grants it.

﴿And if evil befell them, they ascribed it as an omen to Moses and those with him﴾, meaning: they considered Moses a bad omen and said, "This comes from our following you and obeying you," in accordance with the practice of the Arabs, who would scare away birds to read omens: they regarded the *barih* (a bird passing from the left, i.e., from the north) as a bad omen, and they regarded the *sanih* (a bird passing from the right, i.e., from the south) as a blessing. Then He said, refuting their statement:

﴿Indeed, their omen is with Allah﴾, meaning: the omen of blessing and the omen of misfortune are both from Allah.

"A people whose children are busy with lice, and with chains, new ones, and a barred gate."

وَواحِدُ القَمْلِ قَمْلَةٌ.

وَأمّا الضَّفادِعُ فَواحِدُها ḍifdaʿ (frog)، وهو مَشْهُورٌ.

وَقِيلَ إنَّهُ كانَ يُوجَدُ في فِراشِهِمْ وآنِيَتِهِمْ، ويَدْخُلُ في ثِيابِهِمْ فَيَشْتَدُّ أذاهُ لَهم.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 136–137:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And We caused the people who had been considered weak to inherit⦅the eastern and western parts of the land which We had blessed⦆﴾ admits of two meanings. The first: "who were deemed insignificant" (yastaqillun). The second: "who were humiliated" (yastadhilluna), and they were the Children of Israel.

﴿the eastern and western parts of the land﴾ has three opinions concerning it. The first: it means the east and the west. This was said by Ibn Isa.

The second: the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria) and Egypt. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: the land of al-Sham alone, its east and its west. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿which We had blessed﴾ has two opinions concerning it. The first: with fertility.

The second: with an abundance of rivers, trees and fruits.

﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience﴾ has two opinions concerning it. The first: the fulfilment of the "good word" is what He promised them of the destruction of their enemy and their succession in the land, by His saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land﴾. He called it "the good word" because He promised what they loved.

The second: it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We wished to confer favour upon those who were deemed weak in the land, and to make them leaders and to make them the inheritors﴾ and ﴿and to establish them in the land and to show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts from them what they had been fearing﴾ [al-Qasas: 5, 6]. And in His saying ﴿because of their patience﴾ there are two meanings. The first: because of their patience over the harm of Pharaoh.

The second: because of their patience in obedience to Allah.(p-255)

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Indeed, these people — what they are engaged in is destroyed (mutabbarun)﴾. Regarding ﴿mutabbarun﴾ there are three meanings:

First: it means "vain" or "worthless." This was said by al-Kalbi.

Second: it means "misguidance." This was related by Abu al-Yasa'.

Third: it means "destructive," that is, ruinous. From this comes the word tibr, meaning gold (al-dhahab).

As for why it is called by this name, there are two opinions:

One: because Musa will destroy it.

Two: because it is broken, and every broken vessel is called mutabbar. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Al-Dahhak said: it is a Nabataean word, for the reason we have mentioned.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Indeed, these people — what they are engaged in is destroyed (mutabbarun)﴾. Regarding ﴿mutabbarun﴾ there are three meanings:

First: it means "vain" or "worthless." This was said by al-Kalbi.

Second: it means "misguidance." This was related by Abu al-Yasa'.

Third: it means "destructive," that is, ruinous. From this comes the word tibr, meaning gold (al-dhahab).

As for why it is called by this name, there are two opinions:

One: because Musa will destroy it.

Two: because it is broken, and every broken vessel is called mutabbar. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Al-Dahhak said: it is a Nabataean word, for the reason we have mentioned.

The Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾. He said: this reminds them of the blessing.

﴿who afflicted you with the worst torment﴾, that is, the severest torment.

﴿slaughtering your sons and sparing your women﴾, that is, they killed your sons while they were young and spared your women, grown up, for enslavement and servitude.

﴿And in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: what Pharaoh did to you, of killing the sons and enslaving the women, was a tremendous affliction upon you; this is the view of al-Kalbi.

The second: it was a great test and trial for you; this is the view of al-Akhfash.

The third: that your deliverance from that was a tremendous affliction, that is, a great blessing; this is the view of Ibn Qutaybah.(p-256)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 142:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: the thirty nights are a month which he was commanded to fast, and the ten after them are the term (ajal) for his private conversation (munajah) with his Lord.

The second: all forty are the term for his private conversation with his Lord; a term of thirty nights was first set, then ten nights were added after it.

It has also been said that it was Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. This is related from Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, and Masruq.

﴿So the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾. He means that the union of the two terms is the completion of forty nights, so that this shows that the ten are nights and not hours.

If it is said: it is known that the ten together with the thirty make forty, so what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾? There are three answers to this. The first: it is an emphasis in the mention, so it is not impossible. The second: it was His promise to him at the mountain where He spoke to him. The third: to negate that the completion of the thirty by the ten is part of the thirty, because the completion of a thing is a part of it.

If it is said: why did He add ten to the term of His promise after the thirty, making it a second term, and thereby postpone his appointment? It is answered that there are two answers to this. The first: his people were late in coming to him during the first term, so God added to it a second term for them to attend because of their lateness. The second: because his people worshipped the calf after him, so God added a second term to him as a punishment for them.

A third answer is possible: that God did this to him as a test for his people, so that the believer might be distinguished from the hypocrite, and the one who is certain might be known from the doubter.

The difference between al-Miqat and al-Waqt, although they are of one kind, is that al-Miqat is what is determined for an action, whereas al-Waqt may not be determined for an action.

He, may He be exalted and glorified, said: ﴿He said, "My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look at You."﴾ The verse concerns Moses's request to his Lord, and there are three opinions about it.

First, he asked so that God's answer would give him a reply to use against his people when they said: ﴿We will never believe you until we see God plainly﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:55], while Moses knew that it was not permissible to see Him in this world.

Second, he already knew this through reasoning (istidlal, inference), and he wanted to know it by direct necessity (darurah).

Third, he deemed it possible and thought that seeing Him in this world was possible. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi.

God answered him by saying: ﴿"You will not see Me."﴾ Then, in the answer, He showed him what would make clear the impossibility of his request, saying: ﴿"But look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me."﴾ This is because if the mountain cannot remain firm to bear His sight, then a human being is even less able to do so.

﴿When His Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾. The meaning of tajalli (manifestation) is "to appear," derived from jila' al-'arus (the bride's unveiling) when she appears, and from jila' al-mir'ah (the polishing of the mirror) when it becomes bright.

Regarding His manifestation there are four opinions. First, He appeared through the signs He created in the mountain for those present at the mountain. Second, He revealed to the mountain something of His malakut (dominion of the heavens) by which it was crushed, because the world cannot endure what is brought forth from the malakut of the heavens. Third, He displayed an amount the size of the little finger of the Throne. Fourth, His command appeared to the mountain.

﴿He made it crumble﴾. On the word dakkan there are four opinions. First, it means "made level with the earth," derived from the saying naqah dakka' (a she-camel with no hump), said by Ibn Qutaybah and Ibn 'Isa. Second, it sank into the earth, said by al-Hasan and Sufyan. Third, it became dust, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Fourth, it became pieces.

Muqatil said: The greatest mountain in Madyan was broken into six pieces that scattered over the earth. From them, three mountains came to be in Makkah: Thabir, Ghar Thawr and Hira'. In Madinah there are three mountains: Radwa, Uhud and Warqan.

And God knows best.

﴿Moses fell down unconscious﴾. On this there are two opinions. One: he died, said by Qatadah. The other: he fainted, said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

(p-259) Ibn 'Abbas said: He was seized by the swoon from Thursday of the day of 'Arafah, and he recovered on Friday evening. On that day the Torah was revealed to him, and it was the Day of Sacrifice, the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah. In it are ten verses which God sent down in the Qur'an to Muhammad (ﷺ) in the eighteenth surah, Surat Bani Isra'il.

﴿When he recovered, he said, "Glory be to You! I repent to You."﴾ On this there are three opinions. First, he repented of undertaking the request before being permitted to make it. Second, he repented of his belief that seeing Him in this world was permissible. Third, he said this as glorification (tasbih), and it is the custom of believers when signs appear that show the greatness of His power.

﴿"And I am the first of the believers."﴾ On this there are two opinions. One: the first of the believers that none of Your creation can see You, said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. The other: "I am the first of my people to believe, by regarding the request to see You as a grave matter."

And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 144–145:**

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets﴾, the verse. Regarding ﴿And We wrote for him﴾ there are two opinions. The first: We decreed for him, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 183], meaning it was made obligatory.

The second: it is the writing of inscription with a pen on tablets that Allah sent down to him.

They differed about the tablets, of what material they were, in four sayings: (p-260) The first: they were of green emerald (zumurrud), as said by Mujahid.

The second: they were of ruby (yaqut), as said by Ibn Jubayr.

The third: they were of chrysolite (zabarjad), as said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

The fourth: as said by al-Hasan, the tablets were of wood, and the "lawh" (tablet) is derived from the fact that the meanings "shine forth" (talus) through the writing upon it.

Regarding His saying ﴿of everything﴾ there are two opinions: The first: of everything that he needs in his religion, of the lawful and the unlawful, the permitted and the forbidden, the obligatory and the non-obligatory.

The second: He wrote for him in the Tawrah (Torah) of everything of wisdoms and lessons.

Regarding His saying ﴿as an admonition and a detailed explanation﴾ there are two interpretations: The first: the admonition is the prohibitions, and the detailed explanation is the commands, and this is the meaning of the saying of al-Kalbi.

The second: the admonition is the deterrents, and the detailed explanation is the rulings, and this is the meaning of the saying of Muqatil.

He said: and they were seven tablets.

﴿So take it with strength﴾. Regarding this there are four sayings: The first: with earnestness and striving, as said by al-Suddi.

The second: with obedience, as said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The third: with firmness of resolve, as said by Ali ibn Isa.

The fourth: with thankfulness, as said by Juwaybir.

﴿And command your people to take the best of it﴾. He did not say this because some of it is not good. Regarding this there are three interpretations: The first: its best is the obligatory matters, and the non-best is the permitted matters.

The second: it refers to the abrogating (nasikh) ruling, not the abrogated (mansukh) one. (Naskh: abrogation, the replacement of an earlier ruling by a later one.)

(p-261) The third: that doing what one is commanded to do is better than abstaining from what one is forbidden, because action is heavier than abstention, even if abstention is also obedience.

﴿I shall show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾. Regarding this there are four sayings: The first: it is Hell, as said by al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The second: it is the dwellings of those destroyed through denial from 'Ad, Thamud and the earlier generations, so that you may take heed from them and from what they came to of punishment, as said by Qatadah.

The third: they are the dwellings of the tyrannical and giant inhabitants of Syria (al-Sham).

The fourth: it is the house of Pharaoh, which is Egypt.

Qassamah ibn Zuhayr recited: (sa-'uwirithukum) (with the verb in the form "I shall make you inherit").

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 146–147:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant on the earth without right﴾. There are three interpretations of this:

First: I will prevent them from understanding the Qur'an. This was said by Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna.

Second: I will make their punishment for their disbelief the misguidance that keeps them from being guided by what has come to them of the truth.

Third: I will turn them away from warding off punishment from themselves.

Regarding ﴿yatakabbarun﴾ (they are arrogant) there are two interpretations. The first: they belittle people and consider that they have superiority over them.

The second: they are arrogant toward faith and following the Messenger.

﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it; and if they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as a way; but if they see the way of error, they will take it as a way.﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: that "right guidance" (rushd) is faith, and "error" (ghayy) is disbelief.

The second: that "right guidance" (rushd) is guidance, and "error" (ghayy) is misguidance.

﴿That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: heedless of faith.

The second: heedless of the recompense.

﴿That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: heedless of faith.

The second: heedless of the recompense.

[p. 263] The Most High said: ﴿And when Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾. Regarding *asaf* (grief), there are five opinions:

First: it is one who grieves over the loss of what has passed. This was said by Ali ibn Isa.

Second: it is the sorrowful one. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Third: it is one of intense anger. This was said by al-Akhfash.

Fourth: it is one who is enraged. This was said by al-Suddi.

[p. 264] Fifth: it is one who regrets. This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

Concerning his anger and his grief there are two views. One is: he was angry with his people over the worship of the calf, and grieved over what he had missed of conversing with his Lord.

The second is: he was angry with himself for leaving his people until they went astray, and grieved over what he saw among his people of committing acts of disobedience.

Some of the Sufis (mystics) said: his anger was at turning from converse with the Truth to addressing creation.

﴿He said: "Evil is what you have done in my absence after me"﴾, meaning, by worshipping the calf.

﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾ Regarding this there are two views. One: it means the promise of your Lord which He made to me, of forty nights, for they estimated that he had died when he did not come at the end of thirty nights. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

The second: it means the promise of your Lord of reward for His worship, until you turned to worshipping other than Him. This was said by some of the later scholars.

The difference between *'ajala* (haste) and *sur'a* (swiftness) is that *'ajala* is to do something before its time, while *sur'a* is to do it in the least of its times.

﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾. Regarding the reason for throwing them down there are two views. One: out of anger when he saw the worship of the calf. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: he threw them down when he saw in them the virtues of other than his people, of the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), that they are "the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in Allah." He said: "My Lord, make them my nation." He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad." So it weighed heavily upon him, and he threw them down. This was said by Qatada.

The Torah was in seven parts. When Musa threw down the tablets and they shattered, six parts of them were lifted up. Among what was lifted up was the detailing of everything, which Allah mentioned: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets an admonition concerning all things and a detailing of all things﴾. The guidance and mercy remained in the remaining part, which is what Allah mentioned: ﴿He took up the tablets, and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord﴾.

[p. 265] Ibn Abbas said: Musa threw down the tablets and they shattered, and all of them were lifted except a sixth of them.

﴿And he seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward himself﴾. Regarding this there are two views. One: he seized him by the ear. The second: he seized him by the whole of his head.

If it is asked: why did he treat him with such humiliation when he had no sin? There are two answers to this.

One: this act is of a kind whose ruling may change with custom, so it may have been permissible in that time, unlike the humiliation it is regarded as now.

The second: this from him was like a man among us now gripping his beard or biting his lip.

﴿He said: "O son of my mother"﴾. Regarding this there are two views. One: he said that because he was his brother from the same mother. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: he said that according to the custom of the Arabs, to move him through kinship, as the poet said:

"O son of my mother, O very soul of me, you left me to a hard matter."

﴿So do not let the enemies rejoice over me﴾, meaning those who opposed him in worshipping the calf, for by their opposition to him they had become enemies.

﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾, that is: do not be angry with me as You are angry with them, for I am not one of them. Then his tenderness overcame him: ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾

The second: this from him was like a man among us now gripping his beard or biting his lip.

﴿He said: "O son of my mother"﴾. Regarding this there are two views. One: he said that because he was his brother from the same mother. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: he said that according to the custom of the Arabs, to move him through kinship, as the poet said:

"O son of my mother, O very soul of me, you left me to a hard matter."

﴿So do not let the enemies rejoice over me﴾, meaning those who opposed him in worshipping the calf, for by their opposition to him they had become enemies.

﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾, that is: do not be angry with me as You are angry with them, for I am not one of them. Then his tenderness overcame him: ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾

[p. 263] The Most High said: ﴿And when Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾. Regarding *asaf* (grief), there are five opinions:

First: it is one who grieves over the loss of what has passed. This was said by Ali ibn Isa.

Second: it is the sorrowful one. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Third: it is one of intense anger. This was said by al-Akhfash.

Fourth: it is one who is enraged. This was said by al-Suddi.

[p. 264] Fifth: it is one who regrets. This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

Concerning his anger and his grief there are two views. One is: he was angry with his people over the worship of the calf, and grieved over what he had missed of conversing with his Lord.

The second is: he was angry with himself for leaving his people until they went astray, and grieved over what he saw among his people of committing acts of disobedience.

Some of the Sufis (mystics) said: his anger was at turning from converse with the Truth to addressing creation.

﴿He said: "Evil is what you have done in my absence after me"﴾, meaning, by worshipping the calf.

﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾ Regarding this there are two views. One: it means the promise of your Lord which He made to me, of forty nights, for they estimated that he had died when he did not come at the end of thirty nights. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

The second: it means the promise of your Lord of reward for His worship, until you turned to worshipping other than Him. This was said by some of the later scholars.

The difference between *'ajala* (haste) and *sur'a* (swiftness) is that *'ajala* is to do something before its time, while *sur'a* is to do it in the least of its times.

﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾. Regarding the reason for throwing them down there are two views. One: out of anger when he saw the worship of the calf. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: he threw them down when he saw in them the virtues of other than his people, of the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), that they are "the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in Allah." He said: "My Lord, make them my nation." He said: "That is the nation of Ahmad." So it weighed heavily upon him, and he threw them down. This was said by Qatada.

The Torah was in seven parts. When Musa threw down the tablets and they shattered, six parts of them were lifted up. Among what was lifted up was the detailing of everything, which Allah mentioned: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets an admonition concerning all things and a detailing of all things﴾. The guidance and mercy remained in the remaining part, which is what Allah mentioned: ﴿He took up the tablets, and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord﴾.

[p. 265] Ibn Abbas said: Musa threw down the tablets and they shattered, and all of them were lifted except a sixth of them.

﴿And he seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward himself﴾. Regarding this there are two views. One: he seized him by the ear. The second: he seized him by the whole of his head.

If it is asked: why did he treat him with such humiliation when he had no sin? There are two answers to this.

One: this act is of a kind whose ruling may change with custom, so it may have been permissible in that time, unlike the humiliation it is regarded as now.

The second: this from him was like a man among us now gripping his beard or biting his lip.

﴿He said: "O son of my mother"﴾. Regarding this there are two views. One: he said that because he was his brother from the same mother. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: he said that according to the custom of the Arabs, to move him through kinship, as the poet said:

"O son of my mother, O very soul of me, you left me to a hard matter."

﴿So do not let the enemies rejoice over me﴾, meaning those who opposed him in worshipping the calf, for by their opposition to him they had become enemies.

﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾, that is: do not be angry with me as You are angry with them, for I am not one of them. Then his tenderness overcame him: ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 152–154:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And those who did evil deeds and then repented after them and believed﴾. As for repentance from evil deeds, it is regret over what has passed and resolve not to do the like of it.

If it is said: repentance is itself faith, so what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿then repented after them and believed﴾? The answer to this is from three aspects. The first: it means that they repented from disobedience and resumed the work of faith after repentance.

The second: it means that they repented after disobedience and believed through that repentance.

The third: and believed that Allah is accepting of repentance.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 152–154:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And those who did evil deeds and then repented after them and believed﴾. As for repentance from evil deeds, it is regret over what has passed and resolve not to do the like of it.

If it is said: repentance is itself faith, so what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿then repented after them and believed﴾? The answer to this is from three aspects. The first: it means that they repented from disobedience and resumed the work of faith after repentance.

The second: it means that they repented after disobedience and believed through that repentance.

The third: and believed that Allah is accepting of repentance.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 155:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time﴾. In the speech there is an omitted element, and its estimated meaning is: "And Musa chose from among his people seventy men."

Regarding His saying ﴿for Our appointed time﴾ there are two opinions. One of them: it is the appointed time mentioned in the request to see (God).

The second: it is a different appointed time from the first, namely the appointed time of repentance from the worship of the calf.

﴿So when the quake seized them﴾. Regarding it (al-rajfa) there are three aspects. The first: it is the earthquake (al-zalzala), said by al-Kalbi.

The second: it is death. Mujahid said: "They died, then He brought them back to life."

The third: it is a fire that burned them, so Musa thought that they had perished, but they had not perished, said by al-Farra'.

﴿He said: "My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me as well."﴾ Regarding the cause of their being seized, there are two opinions. One: because they had asked to see (God), said by Ibn Ishaq.

(p-266) The second: because they had not forbidden the worship of the calf, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ Regarding it there are two opinions. One: it is an interrogative question out of fear that God had encompassed them with His punishment, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have wronged﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. The second: it is a question of negation, and its estimated meaning is: "Indeed You do not punish except the sinner, so how would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?"

It is related that God caused the seventy whom Musa had chosen from his people to die by the quake, not a death of annihilation, but a death of trial, so that by it He might make firm those who obeyed and take vengeance by it upon those who disobeyed. A swoon seized Musa, then Musa recovered, and God brought the dead back to life. He said: ﴿It is none but Your trial. You lead astray by it whom You will, and You guide whom You will﴾. Regarding it there are two aspects. The first: that by "trial" is meant punishment, said by Qatada.

The second: that by it is meant testing and examination.

"The Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿And prescribe for us good in this world and in the Hereafter﴾. Regarding "good" (ḥasanah) here there are three opinions. The first: it is blessing, and it was called "good" because of how well it is received in souls.

The second: it is good praise.

The third: it is the things deserving of obedience.

﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: its meaning is "we have repented to You." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibrahim.

The second: "we have returned to You in repentance," because it derives from hāda Yahūd (to return), when one returns. This was said by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

The third: meaning "we have drawn near to You through repentance," from their saying: "he has no hawādah (standing) with so-and-so," i.e., he has no means by which he is brought near to him. This was said by Ibn Baḥr.

﴿He said: My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. One: "whom I will of My creation, just as I afflicted your people with it."

The second: "whom I will, in hastening or delaying."

﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: its scope is general but its meaning is specific. The interpretation of this is: "And My mercy has encompassed those among the community of Muhammad ﷺ who believe in Me," based on His saying, ﴿So I will prescribe it for those who fear Allah﴾, the verse. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is general in this world and specific in the Hereafter. The interpretation of this is: "My mercy encompassed in this world the righteous and the wicked, and in the Hereafter it is exclusively for those who fear Allah." This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The third: it is repentance, and it is general. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿So I will prescribe it for those who fear Allah﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. One: they fear shirk (associating partners with Allah). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they fear sins. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿And who give zakah﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. One: it is the zakah on their wealth, because it is among the most difficult of their obligations, and this is the view of the majority.

The second: its meaning is that they obey Allah and His Messenger. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan, who held that it means acting upon what purifies the soul and cleanses it of righteous deeds.

As for the pronoun referred to by the hāʾ in ﴿So I will prescribe it﴾, it has been said that when Musa set out with the delegation of the Children of Israel, Allah spoke to him and said: "Indeed, I have spread the earth for them as a means of purification and as places of prostration, where they may pray wherever the prayer reaches them, except at a latrine, a grave, or a bathhouse. I have placed tranquility (sakinah) in their hearts, and I have made them recite the Torah by heart." He said: So Musa mentioned that to the Children of Israel, and they said: "We cannot bear the tranquility in our hearts, so place it for us in a chest; and we will not recite the Torah except by looking at it, and we will not pray except within the tranquility." Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So I will prescribe it for those who fear Allah and give zakah﴾, meaning what has passed of the tranquility, the prayer, and the recitation. Then He clarified who they are, saying:

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 7, verse 157:

﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet﴾. He means Muhammad ﷺ. Regarding his being called *al-ummi* (the unlettered), there are three opinions. The first: he could not write. The second: it is because he is from *Umm al-Qura* (the Mother of Cities), which is Makkah. The third: it is because among the Arabs there is a people called *ummiyyah* (the unlettered people).

﴿whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾. This is because in the Torah, in the Fifth Book: "I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you, and I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything that I command him."

And in it: "As for the son of the (female) servant, I have blessed him greatly, very greatly, and I will keep him for a great nation."

And in the Gospel there is good news of the *Faraqlit* (Paraclete) in several places: "He will give you another Faraqlit who will be with you forever."

And in it is the saying of the Messiah to the disciples: "I am going away, and the Faraqlit, the Spirit of truth, will come to you, who does not speak from himself. He is your warner; he will combine the truth, inform you of matters to come, praise me, and bear witness to me."

This is the explanation of ﴿they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾. Then He said: ﴿He enjoins on them what is right﴾, which is the truth.

﴿and forbids them what is wrong﴾, which is falsehood. Truth was called *ma'ruf* (what is known) because it is recognized as sound by the intellects, and falsehood was called *munkar* (what is denied) because it is rejected as unsound by the intellects.

(p-269) Then He said: ﴿and makes lawful for them the good things﴾, meaning what the *Jahiliyyah* (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance) used to prohibit, such as the *bahirah*, the *sa'ibah*, the *wasilah* and the *ham*.

﴿and prohibits for them the impure things﴾, meaning what they used to consider lawful, such as the flesh of swine and blood.

﴿and relieves them of their burden﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: it is their covenant that Allah Most High had taken from the Children of Israel.

The second: it is the strictness imposed upon the Children of Israel in their religion, such as the prohibition of the Sabbath, the prohibition of fats and sinews, and other difficult matters. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿and the shackles that were upon them﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: it is the covenant that He took from them concerning what He prohibited for them. This was said by Ibn Abi Talhah.

The second: it means what Allah Most High explained in His saying: ﴿Their hands are chained up﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64].

﴿So those who believed in him and honoured him﴾. Here there are two meanings. The first: it means they revered him. This was said by Ali ibn Isa.

The second: they protected him from his enemies. This was said by Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.

From this comes *ta'zir* (discretionary punishment) for the offender, because it prevents him from returning to the like of his offence.

﴿and followed the light that was sent down with him﴾, meaning the Qur'an, which they believed in after him. Qatadah narrated that the Prophet of Allah ﷺ said to his companions: "Which of creation do you consider most wondrous in faith?" They said: "The angels." The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels are with their Lord, so why would they not believe?"

They said: "The prophets." He said: "Revelation comes to them, so why would they not believe?" They said: "We, O Prophet of Allah."

He said: "I am among you, so why would you not believe?" They said: "O Prophet of Allah, then who are they?" He said: "They are a people who will come after you; they will find a book on a leaf and will believe in it."

This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and followed the light that was sent down with him﴾.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 158–159:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And among the people of Musa is a community that guides by the truth﴾. If it is said: this indicates that among the Jews there are those who are upon the truth.

The answer to this is in three respects. The first: they are those who held fast to the truth at the time of their misguidance, when they killed their prophets, and this does not indicate that their state continued forever.

The second: they are a people beyond China, to whom the call of Islam had not reached. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi.

The third: they are those who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), such as Ibn Salam and Ibn Suriya and others. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 158–159:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And among the people of Musa is a community that guides by the truth﴾. If it is said: this indicates that among the Jews there are those who are upon the truth.

The answer to this is in three respects. The first: they are those who held fast to the truth at the time of their misguidance, when they killed their prophets, and this does not indicate that their state continued forever.

The second: they are a people beyond China, to whom the call of Islam had not reached. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi.

The third: they are those who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), such as Ibn Salam and Ibn Suriya and others. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 160–162:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And when it was said to them, "Dwell in this town"﴾. Scholars differed regarding the root from which the name "qaryah" (town) is derived, giving two views. The first: it is because water is gathered into it (yuqra ilayha), meaning it is collected, from the saying of the people, "qara al-ma' fi hawdihi" (he gathered the water in his basin) when he collected it.

The second: it is because people gather to it, just as water gathers in the basin.

Scholars also differed regarding this town, giving two views. The first: that it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as said by Qatadah.

The second: that it is the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria), as said by al-Hasan.

If it is asked: how did He call the dwelling a "maskan" (dwelling place) when a person moves about in his dwelling? It is answered: because he gives up free activity in it, so he becomes still (sakin) in most of his conditions, even if he is moving in some of them.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea﴾. There are five opinions concerning it.

The first is that it is Ayla. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, and al-Suddi.

The second is that it was on the coast of Madyan. This was said by Qatada.

The third is that it was Madyan, a town between Ayla and al-Tur. Abu Ja'far al-Tabari related this.

The fourth is that it was a town called Maqta, between Madyan and 'Aynuna. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

(p-272) The fifth is what Ibn Shihab said: that the town that was by the sea was Tiberias, and the town of which He said ﴿And present to them a parable: the companions of the town﴾ [Ya-Sin: 13] was Antioch.

Their being asked about this town was a question of rebuke for the earlier sin and the ugly disobedience that they committed there.

﴿When they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾ refers to their transgression in it by doing what they had been forbidden from.

﴿When their fish came to them on their Sabbath day, openly (shurra'an)﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first is that the meaning of ﴿shurra'an﴾ is floating on the water, visible, and from this comes the word shawari' al-balad (the main streets of a town), because of their prominence.

The second is that they came to them from every direction. This was said by 'Ata' al-'Awfi.

The third is that they came in great numbers at their doorways, appearing like white rams raising their heads. This was related by some of the later scholars, and [the people] transgressed and took them on the Sabbath. This was said by al-Hasan.

"His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾ "nasu" means "tarakū" (they abandoned). That by which they had been reminded was to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

﴿We rescued those who forbade evil﴾ and they are those who enjoined what is right and forbade what is wrong.

﴿And We seized those who did wrong﴾ and they are those who abandoned what is right and committed what is wrong.

﴿with a grievous punishment﴾ Concerning "ba'is" there are three interpretations. The first: severe, said by Mujahid.

The second: wretched (radi'), said by al-Akhfash.

The third: that it is the punishment accompanied by poverty, which is hardship (al-bu's).

(p-273) As for the third group, those who neither forbade nor committed the evil, there are two opinions concerning them. The first: that they were rescued along with those who had forbidden it. The second: what Ibn 'Abbas said: "I do not know what was done to them."

"His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾ "nasu" means "tarakū" (they abandoned). That by which they had been reminded was to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

﴿We rescued those who forbade evil﴾ and they are those who enjoined what is right and forbade what is wrong.

The second: wretched (radi'), said by al-Akhfash.

"The words of Him, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: it is from the form tafa''ala of al-idhn (announcement), and its meaning is "He made known," as said by al-Hasan. From this is the verse of al-A'sha:

"The people announced to me, my neighbours, a separation; they cut the rope of one who was familiar and beloved."

The second: its meaning is "He called out and swore," as said by al-Zajjaj.

﴿He would surely send against them﴾, meaning against the Jews, ﴿until the Day of Resurrection, those who would afflict them with a dreadful torment﴾. Those sent are the Arabs, and "dreadful torment" is humiliation and the taking of the jizya (poll-tax), as said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Qatadah.

It is said that the first of the prophets to establish the kharaj (land tax) and collect it was Musa. He collected the kharaj for seven years, and it was said thirteen, and then he withheld it until the Prophet (ﷺ). Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "I prefer that the jizya be sent to the Anbat."

I know of no reasoning for his preference for this except that they are of the people of Bukhtnassar, so they are more intense in retribution, or because it had been taken from them in exchange for its collection, making them more eager for the exchange.

[Translation of Al-Mawardi's commentary on Q. 7:168–170]

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And We divided them in the land into communities﴾, meaning: We scattered them throughout it in groups.

In their being dispersed through the land there are three aspects. The first: an increase in punishment upon them. The second: that their mutual support might be eliminated. The third: that the righteous might be distinguished from the others, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among them are the righteous, and among them are others below that﴾. Then He said: ﴿And We tested them with good things and bad things﴾. In this there are three aspects. The first: with reward and punishment. The second: with blessings and calamities. The third: with fertility and drought.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾. Its meaning: then a succession succeeded them. The word khalf (succession), with the lam unvowelled (khalf), is used in dispraise; and with the lam vowelled (khalaf), it is used in praise.

Abu 'Ubayda said: its meaning is one [and the same], like athar and ithr. The first (khalf, in dispraise) is more apparent, and it is more common in the speech of the poets. One of them said:

"I left behind a succession, would that they had been [good], and not you, [O Death, would that there were] destruction."

Regarding khalf there are two views. One: it means a generation, as said by al-Farra'. The second: that it is the plural of khalif (one who succeeds).

﴿And they inherited the Book﴾: meaning it passed to them by way of inheritance from predecessor to successor. Concerning who they are, there are two views. One: they are the descendants of the Jews, the sons of their (the earlier people's) sons. The Book they inherited is the Torah, as it passed to them. ﴿They take the goods of this lower life﴾: meaning bribery in judgment, according to the consensus. He called it "goods" (ʿaraḍ) because of the brevity of its remaining.

Regarding describing it as "lower" (adnā), there are two views. One: because it is taken in the lower, nearer world (al-dunyā al-dāniya). The second: because it is among the base prohibited things.

﴿And they say: "It will be forgiven us"﴾: this may bear two meanings. One: that it is already forgiven, so we are not held accountable for it. The second: that it is a sin, but Allah may forgive it for us, their hoping for His mercy.

﴿And if there comes to them goods like it, they will take it﴾: in this there are two views. One: that they are people persistent in sins, as said by Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi. The second: that nothing satisfies them, so they take it not out of need, as said by al-Hasan.

﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them, that they should not say about Allah except the truth?﴾ This may bear two meanings. One: that they should not say about Allah except the truth concerning the prohibition of judging by bribery. The second: concerning all acts of obedience and disobedience, commands and prohibitions.

﴿And they studied what is in it﴾: in this there are two interpretations. One: they abandoned acting upon what is in it, until it became obsolete (dāris). The second: they had recited it and studied it, so they were not ignorant of what is in it, yet they stood opposing it while knowing it.

[Translation of Al-Mawardi's commentary on Q. 7:168–170]

(p-276) His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And when We shook the mountain over them﴾. In this there are three opinions.

The first: We shook it violently (za'za'nahu). This was said by Ibn Qutaybah, and from it is the verse of al-'Ajjaj:

They tested our noble characters,
and they shook our weighty dispositions.

The second: it means We pulled it up (jadhabnahu). Nataq means pulling, and from it the fertile woman is called nathiq. al-Nabigha said:

They did not deprive [their children] of good nourishment, and their mother
overflowed over you with a male-producing fertile one (nathiq).

It has been disputed why she is called nathiq. It was said because the emergence of her offspring is like a pulling. It was also said because she draws in the male's water and brings it forth as a child.

The third: its meaning is "and We raised it over them from its base." al-Farra' said: He raised the mountain over their camp, a farsakh by a farsakh (a parasang in length and breadth).

Mujahid said: The reason for raising the mountain over them was that they refused to accept the obligations of the Torah because of the hardship in them. Musa admonished them but they did not accept, so the mountain was raised above them, and it was said to them: "If you take it with earnestness and striving, well and good; otherwise it will be dropped upon you."

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: So they took it with strength, then afterwards they broke their covenant.

It has been disputed concerning the reason for raising the mountain over them: was it a punishment against them or a favour upon them? There are two opinions. The first: it was a punishment, through the fear that entered them. The second: it was a favour, since they desisted from disobedience because of it.

﴿And they thought that it was going to fall upon them﴾. In this there are two opinions. The first: that it prevailed in their souls that it was going to fall upon them, in the literal sense of thinking (ghalib). The second: that they were certain of it, because of what they witnessed of its being raised over them. This was said by al-Hasan.

(p-277) ﴿Take what We have given you﴾, meaning the Torah.

﴿with strength﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: with earnestness and striving. The second: with a sincere intention and sincere obedience.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants﴾. Scholars differ regarding those whom He brought forth and from whom He took this covenant, on two views. The first: He brought forth the souls before the creation of the bodies and placed in them the knowledge by which they recognised the One who addressed them.

Those who hold this view differ as to whether this occurred before the souls descended to the earth, on two views. The first: it occurred in Paradise before their descent to the earth. The second: He did it after their descent to it.

(p-٢٧٨) The second view, in its basic form, is that He created the souls and the bodies together, and that this took place on earth, according to all who hold this interpretation (ta'wil).

On this view there are two opinions. (p-٢٧٩) The first: He brought them forth like particles (al-dharr, tiny specks) and inspired them, so they spoke this. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: This is because God wiped the back of Adam between Mecca and al-Ta'if, and from the right side of his back there came forth descendants like white particles, and they are the People of the Right. And from the left side of his back there came forth descendants like black particles, and they are the People of the Left. When they all bore witness against themselves, both those among them who believed and those who disbelieved, He returned them.

The second: He brought forth the descendants generation after generation and age after age.

Regarding ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves: Am I not your Lord?﴾ there are two opinions. The first: it means that He pointed them to themselves through what they witnessed of His power; this was said by some of the theologians (mutakallimun).

The second: it means that He made them bear witness against themselves to what they acknowledged of His lordship and His oneness.

On the interpretation, there are two opinions. The first: He said this to the fathers among the Children of Adam when He brought forth their descendants from their backs and made them testify against themselves, "Am I not your Lord?", so as to inform them that He created their descendants after they had not existed, and that He was the Creator of them, because they were descendants like those before them, just as these have become descendants of them. So they acknowledged this when the proof became manifest to them. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The second opinion: He said this to the descendants when He took them from the loins of their fathers. This is the view of the majority. On this view there are two opinions. The first: He said to them, ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ through the tongues of the prophets after their intellects had become complete.

The second: He placed in them intellects by which they knew this, and so they bore witness to it against themselves.

Regarding the root of "dhurriyyah" (descendants), there are two opinions. The first: because they come forth from the loins like particles (dharr). The second: it is derived from "dhara'a Allahu al-khalq", meaning when God brings creation into being and manifests them.
