"The Word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And recite to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them﴾. In this there are three opinions. The first: he is Bal'am ibn Ba'ura (Bal'am ibn Ba'ura), and they differed about him. It was said that he was from Yemen, and it was said that he was from the Canaanites, and it was said that he was from the Banu Sal ibn Lut. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: he is Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt al-Thaqafi. This is related from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr.

The third: he is one of the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam and then became a hypocrite. This is related from Ikrima.

Regarding the signs that he was given, there are three opinions. The first: it is the Greatest Name of Allah, by which supplications are answered. This is related from al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they are a book from the books of Allah. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: he was given prophethood, but his people bribed him to remain silent, so he did so and left them as they were. This is related from Mujahid, and it is not correct, because Allah does not choose for His prophethood anyone whom He knows will depart from His obedience to disobedience.

(p-280) As for His words: ﴿he detached himself from them﴾, there are two meanings. The first: he detached himself from knowledge of them, because he would be stripped of what he was given of them through disobedience.

The second: he detached himself from them, that is, from obedience, through disobedience, while his knowledge of the signs remained, to the point that it is related that Bal'am was bribed to invoke destruction upon the people of Musa, so he slipped and invoked against his own people, and they were destroyed.

﴿So Satan pursued him﴾. In this there are three meanings. The first: Satan made him a follower of himself by his acceptance of him when he misled him.

The second: Satan has followers from among mankind in his misguidance of disbelief.

The third: Satan overtook him and misled him. It is said: "I followed the people" when I caught up with them, and "I trailed them" when I walked behind them. This is related from Ibn Qutayba.

﴿So he became of the misguided﴾. In this there are two meanings. The first: of those who perished.

The second: of those who went astray.

The Word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾. In this there are two meanings. The first: that is, We would have caused him to die, so he would not have disbelieved.

The second: We would have placed between him and disbelief a barrier, so he would attain the exalted station, protected. This is related from Mujahid.

﴿But he clung to the earth﴾, that is, he inclined toward it.

Regarding his inclination toward it, there are two meanings. The first: he inclined toward its people, in their drawing him down and their deceiving him.

The second: he inclined toward the desires of the earth, which occupied him from obedience to Allah. This is clarified by the words of the Exalted: ﴿and followed his desire﴾. Then He struck his likeness to the dog: ﴿If you drive it away, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants﴾. In the comparison to the panting dog there are two meanings. The first: because of its lowliness and humiliation.

The second: because the panting of the dog does not benefit it."

The second: because the panting of the dog does not benefit it."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 178–179:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind﴾. ﴿We have created for Hell﴾ means: We created, from among those who will go to Hell because of their disbelief and disobedience.

As for ﴿many of the jinn and mankind﴾, there are two opinions concerning it. The first: it refers to the children of adultery (awlad al-zina), because they were created from corrupt drops (nutaf khabitha), so they are the people most quick to disbelief and disobedience, and thus they come to combine corruption of belief (su' al-mu'taqad) and corruption of birth (khubth al-mawlid).

The second opinion: it is general, covering the children of adultery and of lawful marriage alike, concerning whoever was born from a marriage or from fornication, because they are held accountable for their own actions, not for their births which were corrupted by the actions of others.

﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand﴾ the truth.

﴿And they have eyes with which they do not see﴾ the right guidance.

﴿And they have ears with which they do not hear﴾ admonition. Thus, by abandoning their use, they are in the position of one who has lost them. Miskin al-Darimi said:

I am blind when my neighbour goes out, until the walls conceal my neighbour,
And deaf to what passes between us, though my hearing is not impaired.

(p-282) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And to God belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: All of His names are beautiful (ḥusnā). Regarding what is meant by "beautiful" here, there are two opinions:

One: that which hearts incline toward when His remembrance is made with pardon and mercy, rather than wrath and vengeance.

The second: His names which He deserves for His own essence and for His acts, among which are attributes that are the path to knowing Him. They are nine:
The Eternal (al-Qadīm), the First before everything.
The Everlasting (al-Bāqī), after the annihilation of everything.
The Able (al-Qādir), whom nothing can overcome.
The All-Knowing (al-ʿĀlim), from whom nothing is hidden.
The Living (al-Ḥayy), who does not die.
The One (al-Wāḥid), "there is nothing like unto Him."
The All-Hearing (al-Samīʿ), the All-Seeing (al-Baṣīr), from whom nothing escapes.
The Self-Sufficient (al-Ghanī), independent of everything.

Regarding calling upon Him by them, there are two opinions: One: calling Him by them when desiring Him in supplication and request.

The second: glorifying Him by them, worshipping Him through mentioning them.

﴿And leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾. In it there are three interpretations: One: its meaning is "they lie," said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: "they associate partners (with Him)," said by Qatadah.

The third: "they distort," said by al-Akhfash.

Regarding their deviation concerning them, there are two opinions: One: their deriving their gods from the names of God, as they named some of them al-Lāt, deriving it from Allah, and some of them al-ʿUzzā, deriving it from al-ʿAzīz, said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

The second: their naming the idols "gods" (ālihah), and naming God, Mighty and Majestic, "the father of the Messiah" and "ʿUzayr."

(p-283) His, may He be exalted and majestic, saying: ﴿And among those whom We created is a community who guide by the truth﴾. Concerning them there are two opinions. The first: they are the scholars (ʿulamāʾ).

The second: they are this Ummah (community).

Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj related this from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 182–183:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who deny Our signs, We will lead them step by step (sanastadrijuhum) from where they do not know﴾. Istidraj (gradual drawing-on, leading someone step by step) is that one is carried through one state after another, each state lower than the last.

Regarding its derivation there are two opinions. The first: it is derived from daraj (a step, a stair), because it involves one thing after another.

The second: it is derived from darajah (a rank, a degree), because one descends from one rank to another.

Regarding what is referred to by "their istidraj" there are two opinions. The first: their being led step by step to ruin (halakah).

The second: disbelief (kufr).

His saying: ﴿from where they do not know﴾ may carry two meanings. The first: they do not know by means of the istidraj. The second: they do not know of the ruin.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 184–186:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Whomever Allah leads astray, there is no guide for him﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

One of them: the meaning of "yudlilhu" (He leads him astray) is that He judges him to be in error regarding the religion.

The second: He leads him astray from the path of Paradise to the Fire.

﴿And He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾. And "tughyan" (transgression) is excessive aggression.

Regarding ﴿ya'mahun﴾ (wandering blindly) there are two views: One of them: they are bewildered (yatahayyaruna), and "al-'amah" (blind confusion) in the heart is like "al-'ama" (blindness) in the eye.

The second: they hesitate and waver (yataraddadun). This was said by Qutrub, who cited the verse of the poet:

"Whenever he wanders blindly toward Uthman, he wanders blindly toward the big-canopied and the caravan-driver."

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 187:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the Hour, when it will occur﴾. There are two opinions regarding it. The first: those who asked about it were the Jews. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: those who asked about it were the Quraysh. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

﴿Ayyana mursaha﴾. As for أيّان (ayyan), it means "when" (matā), and from it is the saying of the rajaz poet:

*When will He fulfill my need, when?*
*Do you not see that its time has come for its success?*

As for ﴿mursaha﴾ (مُرْساها), there are three opinions regarding it. The first: its establishment (qiyamuha). This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: its end (muntahaha). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: its appearance (zuhuruha). This was said by al-Akhfash.

(p-285) ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal its time except Him﴾. None knows its time except Him, denying that anyone other than God knows it. ﴿It has been heavy upon the heavens and the earth﴾. There are three interpretations regarding it. The first: the coming of the Hour was grievous to the people of the heavens and the earth. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: its establishment was burdensome for them. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: its meaning is that its description was momentous to the people of the heavens and the earth. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾. He means while they are heedless, because no one knows it except God, and no reports about it came from God. So its coming is sudden, and that is more severe for it, as the poet said:

*And the most painful thing is when the sudden event strikes you unexpectedly.*

﴿They ask you as if you were eager about it﴾. There are two interpretations regarding it. The first: its meaning is "knowing about it." This was said by Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, and Maʿmar.

The second: the meaning of the speech is "they ask you about it as if you were fond of them," by inversion of word order, meaning that you have an affection between you and them that obliges you to show them kindness, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, He has been ever kind to me﴾ [Maryam: 46]. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on surah 7, verse 188:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Say: I possess not for myself any benefit or harm﴾, meaning: I do not possess the power over them without any preventer or repeller.

﴿Except what Allah wills﴾, that He should give me possession of it, so I possess it by His will.

﴿And had I known the unseen, I would have acquired much of good﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: I would have acquired much of righteous deeds; this was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: I would have stored up from the fertile year for the barren year; this was said by al-Farra'.

The third, and it is anomalous: I would have bought when prices were low and sold when prices were high.

(p-286) ﴿And harm would not have touched me﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: there is no madness in me, as the polytheists claimed; this was said by al-Hasan.

The second: poverty would not have touched me, because of my acquiring much of good.

The third: I would not have fallen into doubt.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 189–190:

﴿So when He gave them a good child, they made for Him partners in what He had given them.﴾ This is because Iblis said to Hawwa', "Name him 'Abd al-Harith," meaning himself, for his name in the heavens was al-Harith. So she named him 'Abd Allah, and he died. Then she conceived a second child, and he told her this again, but she did not accept it, and he died. Then she conceived a third, and he said to her and to Adam, "Do you think God will leave His servant with you? No, by God, He will surely take him as He took the others." So they named him by that name, and he lived. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿they made for Him partners in what He had given them﴾, that is, in the name. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "He deceived them twice: he deceived them in Paradise, and he deceived them on earth."

(p-287) al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the one referred to by His words ﴿they made for Him partners in what He had given them﴾ is the son of Adam and his wife, and it does not refer back to Adam and Hawwa'.

The Words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?﴾ He means the idols: "Do they have feet with which they walk in your interests?"

﴿Or do they have hands with which they strike?﴾ That is, in repelling [harm] from you.

﴿Or do they have eyes with which they see?﴾ That is, [they see] your harm from your benefit.

﴿Or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ [They hear] your supplication and your humble pleading.

If it is said: Why did He denounce the worship of one who has no feet, no hands, and no eyes? It is answered: there are two responses to this. The first: whoever worships a body that does not benefit is more blameworthy than whoever worships a body that does benefit.

The second: He informed them that they are superior to them, so how can they worship one who is inferior to them?

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 199–200:

The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿Take what is easy (al-'afw)﴾ have three interpretations. The first: al-'afw refers to the good character and conduct of people. This was said by Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, and Mujahid.

The second: "Take the 'afw from the wealth of the Muslims." This was before the obligation of zakat, and then it was abrogated (naskh) by it. This was said by al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and one of the two opinions of Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: "Take the 'afw from the polytheists." This was before the obligation of jihad. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿And enjoin what is good (al-'urf)﴾ has two opinions. The first: its meaning is "what is known as good (al-ma'ruf)." This was said by 'Urwah and Qatadah.

The second: what was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when this verse was revealed to him, ﴿Take what is easy and enjoin what is good﴾, he said to Jibril: "O Jibril, what is this?" He said: "I do not know until I ask the One who knows." Then Jibril returned and said: "O Muhammad, your Lord commands you to join the one who cuts you off, to give to the one who withholds from you, and to pardon the one who wrongs you." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾. If it is asked: how can he be commanded to turn away while it is obligatory to rebuke them? It is said: he only meant turning away from the foolish, showing disdain toward them.

And this, although it is an address to his Prophet (peace be upon him), is a form of discipline for all of his creation.

The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should tempt you (nazgh)﴾ have three meanings. The first: al-nazgh is being disturbed or agitated. The second: anger. The third: temptation (al-fitnah), said by Muqatil.

(p-289) ﴿So seek refuge in Allah; indeed, He is Hearing, Knowing﴾. Hearing of the ignorance of those who are ignorant, Knowing of what removes the nazgh from you.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 201–202:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, those who are mindful of God—when an evil whisper from Satan touches them﴾. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read ﴿ta'if﴾, while the rest read (tayf). Scholars differed about these two readings according to two views.

The first: the two readings have one meaning, even though the wording differs. On this view, scholars differed in interpreting it in four ways:

First: the tayf is the lamam (a passing touch of wrongdoing), like a phantom that visits a person.

Second: it is the waswasah (whispering), said by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'.

Third: it is anger, the view of Mujahid.

Fourth: it is fear, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second view: the meanings of tayf and ta'if differ. The tayf is the lamam, while the ta'if is everything that circles around a person.

﴿They remember, and then they are seeing clearly﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One: they came to know, and then they are refraining.

The second: they took heed, and then they are guided.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 201–202:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, those who are mindful of God—when an evil whisper from Satan touches them﴾. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read ﴿ta'if﴾, while the rest read (tayf). Scholars differed about these two readings according to two views.

The first: the two readings have one meaning, even though the wording differs. On this view, scholars differed in interpreting it in four ways:

First: the tayf is the lamam (a passing touch of wrongdoing), like a phantom that visits a person.

Second: it is the waswasah (whispering), said by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'.

Third: it is anger, the view of Mujahid.

Fourth: it is fear, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second view: the meanings of tayf and ta'if differ. The tayf is the lamam, while the ta'if is everything that circles around a person.

﴿They remember, and then they are seeing clearly﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One: they came to know, and then they are refraining.

The second: they took heed, and then they are guided.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say, "Why have you not chosen it?"﴾ There are three interpretations of this:

First: its meaning is, "Why did you not bring it to us from yourself?" This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

Second: its meaning is, "Why did you not choose it for yourself?"

Third: its meaning is, "Why did you not receive it from your Lord?" This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verse 204:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, means: to its recitation.

﴿And be silent﴾ means: do not respond to it with speech or with inattention. ﴿That you may be shown mercy﴾.

The scholars differed regarding the situation to which this listening-and-silence applies, in three opinions:

The first: it was revealed concerning the one following the imam (al-ma'mum) who listens and does not recite. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it was revealed concerning the Friday sermon (khutbah), where those present listen to it and do not speak. This was said by ʿĀʾishah and ʿAṭāʾ.

The third: what Ibn Mas'ud said: "We used to greet one another during the prayer, saying, 'Peace be upon so-and-so, peace be upon so-and-so,' until the Qur'an came down with: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent.﴾"

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 7, verses 205–206:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself⦾﴾. In this remembrance there are three aspects. The first: it is the remembrance of recitation in prayer behind the imam, silently within oneself, as said by Qatadah.

The second: it is a remembrance by the heart, by sustaining reflection so that one does not forget the blessings of Allah which necessitate obedience to Him.

(p-291) The third: remembering Him with the tongue, either out of desire for Him in supplication, or out of exalting Him through the verse.

Regarding the one addressed by this remembrance, there are two opinions. The first: he is the listener to the Qur'an, whether in prayer or in the khutbah, as said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, and its meaning is general for all the responsible.

Then He said: ﴿humbly and with fear﴾. As for tadarru' (humility), it is lowliness and submissiveness; as for khifah (fear), its meaning is dread of Him.

﴿and without loudness in speech﴾, meaning: a speech kept quiet, either in the heart or with the tongue, according to the two interpretations previously mentioned.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾. In this there are two aspects. The first: in the early and the late parts of the day.

The second: al-ghuduww is the end of dawn, which is the Subh prayer, and al-asal is the end of the afternoon, which is the 'Asr prayer; this was said by Mujahid, and similar was reported from Qatadah.

﴿And do not be among the heedless⦾﴾ may bear two meanings: the first: heedless of the remembrance.

The second: heedless of obedience to Him in all His commands and prohibitions; this was said by the majority.

﴿They glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate⦾﴾. This is the first prostration of recitation in the Qur'an.

The occasion of its revelation is what the disbelievers of Makkah said: ﴿And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?⦾ and it increased them in aversion﴾ [al-Furqan: 60]. So Allah revealed this verse and informed them that if the angels brought near are in this state of humility and eagerness, then you are more deserving of that. And Allah knows best what is correct.
